45.title: As for Me and My House, We Will Serve the LORD

mem.t: If it seems evil to you to serve the LORD, choose today whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell; but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.”

s: Together, choose a corner of your home for worship. Place a Bible there; you might also add a candle or a photo of the two of you.
Hold one time of family worship using “Sing, Read, Share, Pray”: sing a song, read Joshua 24:15, and each share one thing you’re thankful for.
Together, write out “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” and put it up by your front door or in that corner.
Hold hands and pray, formally placing this home into the Lord’s hands.

lessons.title: Choose Today
lessons.theme: The direction of a home is a choice to be made today

v: “Now therefore fear the LORD, and serve him in sincerity and in truth. Put away the gods which your fathers served beyond the River, in Egypt; and serve the LORD.

If it seems evil to you to serve the LORD, choose today whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell; but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.”

lessons.still: Be still, and picture two roads leading from your front door. Tell the Lord: “Lord, today we choose to follow you.” Whether or not your family is walking with you yet, you can make this choice for yourself first.
lessons.light: 321 Light: One of our purposes is to build God’s order, and lived out at home, that means building a household that belongs to God. For a home to belong to God, Jesus must first reign there, not work, phones, or our children’s futures. Change begins with me: when I choose first, our home has a direction.
lessons.jesus: Jesus stayed at Zacchaeus’ house, and after Zacchaeus repented, Jesus said, “Today, salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:9). When salvation comes to a person, it comes to their household too. Jesus loves to enter people’s homes, and today he is willing to come into ours and be the Lord of our home.
lessons.pray: Faithful God, you have led us all the way to today. Today we choose before you: as for us and our house, we will serve you. Remove from our hearts everything that competes with you for first place, and make our home a home that worships you and where you reign. Amen.
teach: In his old age, Joshua gathered all Israel, recounted how God had led them all the way, and then asked them to make a choice: “choose today whom you will serve” (Joshua 24:15). Before them were the gods their fathers had served beyond the River, and the gods of the Amorites in whose land they lived. The first are like the old ways of our family of origin; the second, like the currents of the surrounding culture. Every home stands at a crossroads like this.

Today’s “other gods” aren’t necessarily idols; they might be achievement, money, our children’s grades, other people’s opinions, or a comfortable life. Joshua said, “Now therefore fear the LORD, and serve him in sincerity and in truth” (Joshua 24:14). In the original language, the word “serve” also carries the sense of worship. Whatever a home worships, it will be shaped by. A family altar is a clear declaration at home of whom this home belongs to.

Joshua’s most beautiful words are these: “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Joshua 24:15). Notice that he says “me” first, then “my house.” A home’s spiritual direction begins with one person’s decision. If your spouse isn’t yet walking alongside you, you can still be the Joshua of your home, serving the Lord quietly and steadfastly, and drawing your family by your life. A family altar doesn’t begin with a perfect family; it begins with one willing person.
q: Besides God, what else is quietly “being served” in our home, taking up most of our time and attention?
Am I willing to make the choice “I will serve the LORD” first, without waiting for others to start?
talk: If our home could have only one core value written by the door, what would you want it to be?
What one “other god” does our home most need to “put away”? How can we start? (If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down your prayer for this home.)
acts: Write out Joshua 24:15 and post it by your front door
Together, name one “other god” you will put away
Tonight, say together: “Lord, this home belongs to you.”
lessons.noon: “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” — Lord, right now I choose once again to serve you.

lessons.title: Tent and Altar
lessons.theme: Wherever we go, we build an altar to God there

v: The LORD appeared to Abram and said, “I will give this land to your offspring.” He built an altar there to the LORD, who had appeared to him.
He left from there to go to the mountain on the east of Bethel and pitched his tent, having Bethel on the west, and Ai on the east. There he built an altar to the LORD and called on the LORD’s name.
Abram moved his tent, and came and lived by the oaks of Mamre, which are in Hebron, and built an altar there to the LORD.

lessons.still: Think of the homes you’ve lived in since you married, the jobs you’ve changed, the seasons you’ve walked through. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, in each place, did we build an altar to you?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The tent is temporary; the altar points to eternity. When we turn from earth to heaven, from the temporary to the eternal, we won’t be busy only with our tent and forget the altar. When our home’s focus is on Jesus, life has a center: first be with God, then be with people.
lessons.jesus: The Samaritan woman asked on which mountain people should worship. Jesus answered that “the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4:23). Worship isn’t about the place, but about the heart. Jesus shows us that the living room, the dining table, the kitchen, wherever there is a sincere heart, can all become places of worship.
lessons.pray: God of Abraham, thank you for walking with us through every season of our lives. Let us not be busy only pitching tents, but build an altar to you in our home. Wherever we live and whatever our circumstances, make our home a place that calls on your name. Amen.
teach: Two things followed Abram throughout his life: a tent and an altar. He pitched his tent, and “There he built an altar to the LORD and called on the LORD’s name” (Genesis 12:8). The tent stands for daily life: eating, sleeping, working, moving. The altar stands for worship: meeting God and offering ourselves. Tents move and wear out, but the altar makes every place we settle a place of God’s presence.

Many families have only a tent and no altar: life is busy, houses keep getting bigger, yet there are few moments at home of meeting God. Every time Abram came to a new place, he built an altar again; when he reached Hebron, he “built an altar there to the LORD” (Genesis 13:18). A family altar isn’t a ritual but a rhythm of life: wherever we move and whatever season we are in, we keep a place for God.

Today a family altar might be a dining table, a corner of the couch, or the bedside before sleep. It doesn’t need to be big, but it does need to be regular: a set time and a set place, so the family knows, “This is when we meet with God.” Newlyweds can start with just the two of them; families with children can gather everyone; empty-nest couples can begin again. What matters is not the form, but coming before God with one heart.
q: Is our home life right now more like “only a tent,” or “a tent and an altar”?
In past seasons of my life, in what place did God meet me in a special way?
talk: If we chose one place in our home as our “altar,” where would you choose? Why?
Since we married, in the homes we’ve lived in and the seasons we’ve gone through, what graces are worth remembering?
acts: Together, choose a spot in your home for your “altar”
Place a Bible and a prayer card there
Write down one grace God gave you in one of the homes you’ve lived in
lessons.noon: “There he built an altar to the LORD and called on the LORD’s name” — Lord, right now, right where I am, I call on your name.

lessons.title: First, Become Spiritual Companions
lessons.theme: Husband and wife are each other’s most important spiritual companions on earth

v: They were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately.

lessons.still: Think about what your spouse is like spiritually: when they pray, when they read Scripture, when they feel weak. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, make us not only partners in life, but spiritual companions too.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Spiritually, the self-ruled person easily compares: “I’m more spiritual than you,” or “You never lead.” The self-emptied person only asks, “How can I walk with you toward the Lord?” In practicing 920, my spouse is my most important “2”; as I practice the “0” of self-emptying with them, I will bear the “9”-fold fruit of the Spirit.
lessons.jesus: The risen Jesus walked with two disciples and explained the Scriptures to them. Afterward they said to each other, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32). Jesus loves to join two people on the road and set their hearts burning together.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for being willing to walk with us. Make us as husband and wife one in heart before you, spiritual companions to each other, not comparing, not judging, only supporting one another. Set our hearts burning together, and make our home a place that welcomes and blesses others. Amen.
teach: Scripture describes Zechariah and Elizabeth this way: “They were both righteous before God” (Luke 1:6). The word “both” is beautiful: they didn’t each walk their own spiritual path, but stood together before God. They also went through many years of waiting, yet they didn’t leave God in their disappointment, nor did they leave each other. The first step of a family altar is not leading others, but husband and wife first becoming spiritual companions.

Priscilla and Aquila are a couple who always appear together in the New Testament. When they heard Apollos preach, “they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately” (Acts 18:26). They worked together, welcomed people together, and taught together; their home was the place of their ministry. This is the “2” in 235: spiritual companions. When husband and wife become spiritual companions, the family altar has two solid pillars.

Being spiritual companions isn’t about who is more spiritual, nor about one being the other’s teacher. Perhaps one knows the Bible better and the other is better at prayer; perhaps one has just come to faith and the other has walked with God for many years. Companions walk side by side; they don’t grade each other. You can start simply: each day, share one verse, one thing you’re thankful for, and one prayer request. If your spouse doesn’t yet believe or isn’t yet willing, you can first be their spiritual watchman, quietly praying for them.
q: Have I ever compared myself spiritually with my spouse, or been disappointed that they’re “not spiritual enough”?
How can I be my spouse’s spiritual companion, rather than their spiritual teacher or judge?
talk: On the journey of faith, what is the one thing you’re most thankful to me for?
What is the simplest spiritual habit we could start practicing together? (If your spouse can’t join you for now, write down what you’ll pray as you watch over them.)
acts: Today, share with your spouse a verse that has touched you
Ask your spouse: “How can I pray for you?”
Together, think of one person you could welcome or care for
lessons.noon: “They were both righteous before God” — Lord, right now let the two of us stand together before you.

lessons.title: Family Worship Can Be Simple
lessons.theme: Sing, Read, Share, Pray: a fifteen-minute family altar

v: I will bless the LORD at all times. His praise will always be in my mouth.
My soul shall boast in the LORD. The humble shall hear of it and be glad.
Oh magnify the LORD with me. Let’s exalt his name together.
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your heart to the Lord.

lessons.still: Softly hum a hymn you know well, or silently say a line of praise in your heart, and let your heart turn from busyness toward God. Tell the Lord: “Lord, together we will exalt your name.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The goal of family worship is not to prove how spiritual our family is, but to let Jesus receive all the glory. As we exalt his name together, our focus shifts from ourselves, our spouse, and our problems to God, and the atmosphere at home turns from scorekeeping to gratitude.
lessons.jesus: After the Last Supper, Matthew tells us, “When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives” (Matthew 26:30). On the heaviest night of all, Jesus sang with his own. Family worship can be like this too: gathered around the table, simply singing together and giving our hearts to God together.
lessons.pray: Lord, you are worthy of all praise. Help us stop seeing family worship as a burden, and see it instead as the joy of gathering with you together. Let the word of Christ dwell richly in our hearts, and fill our home with songs, Scripture, thanksgiving, and prayer. Amen.
teach: David says, “Oh magnify the LORD with me. Let’s exalt his name together” (Psalm 34:3). The words “with me” and “together” capture the very spirit of family worship. Many families don’t lack the desire to worship; they just find it too hard, too formal, and don’t know where to start. Actually, family worship can be like a home-cooked meal: it doesn’t need to be a feast, but it should be nourishing, and we should have it often.

Paul gives us a simple framework: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs” (Colossians 3:16). We can remember it with four words: Sing, Read, Share, Pray. Sing a song; read a passage of Scripture; share what it means to us, along with something we’re thankful for; and finally pray together. Fifteen minutes is one family altar.

A few practical reminders. First, short and regular beats long and irregular. Second, keep the atmosphere relaxed: it’s not a Bible study, and certainly not a lecture. Third, families with children can let the children pick songs and read Scripture; couples on their own can take turns leading. Fourth, if you miss a week, don’t beat yourself up; just start again the next week. What matters most in family worship is not performance, but letting the family experience God together.
q: What has kept us from starting family worship: time, awkwardness, or not knowing how?
During the week, do I myself have a regular time of blessing God?
talk: If we chose a “family song” for our home, which one would you choose? Why?
What day and time would work best for our family to worship? Who will lead the first time?
acts: Choose a “family song” together
Set a time for family worship this week
Hold your first fifteen-minute worship time using Sing, Read, Share, Pray
lessons.noon: “His praise will always be in my mouth” — Lord, right now I will bless you; let your praise always be in my mouth.

lessons.title: The Fire on the Altar Must Not Go Out
lessons.theme: A family altar needs steady tending, and sometimes rekindling

v: Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out.
Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart,
praising God and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.

lessons.still: Picture a bed of coals: if no wood is added, the fire slowly dies down. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, how is the fire in my heart for you burning right now?” Whether it’s a blazing fire or just a few embers, bring it to him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Fires usually go out not because of a great wind, but because no one adds wood. When we rely on our own enthusiasm, the fire flares and fades; when we live from the heart by the Spirit, the fire keeps burning. Letting Jesus reign is not a one-time decision, but a choice we make again every day.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus returned to Nazareth, “He entered, as was his custom, into the synagogue on the Sabbath day” (Luke 4:16). His life had a regular rhythm of worship, part of his close fellowship with the Father. Jesus shows us that spiritual life needs steady practice, not just occasional bursts of enthusiasm.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, kindle a fire in our home that keeps on burning. When we are tired, busy, or weak, add wood to the fire for us again. Make our home like the homes of the early church, full of gladness, sincerity, and praise, so that people come to know you through our home. Amen.
teach: God commanded the priests, “Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out” (Leviticus 6:13). Every morning the priests had to add wood and clear away the ashes so the fire would keep burning. A family altar is the same: starting isn’t hard; keeping it going is. Enthusiasm fades, time gets squeezed, seasons of life change; someone needs to add another piece of wood every day, every week.

Day by day, the believers in the early church kept “continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home” (Acts 2:46). Their faith wasn’t only in their gatherings but also around the dinner table at home. “They took their food with gladness and singleness of heart, praising God” (Acts 2:46–47), and the result was that “The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved” (Acts 2:47). Worship at home ultimately becomes a witness that draws people to the Lord.

How do we keep the fire burning? First, set a rhythm: put family worship on the calendar. Second, stay flexible: when traveling or busy, even five minutes of prayer is good. Third, when the fire burns low, rekindle it; don’t give up because you’ve missed a few weeks. Fourth, record what God has done; looking back will stir up your faith. Looking back on this week: choosing to serve, tent and altar, spiritual companions, simple worship, tending the flame. Our home is becoming a place of God’s presence.
q: Have we ever started a spiritual habit that later died out? What was the reason?
In our family altar, which part am I willing to take responsibility for, “adding the wood”?
talk: This week, what moment in our family worship did you enjoy most?
When the fire burns low, how can we remind each other and rekindle it?
acts: Put your family worship time on the calendar
Start a “grace journal” and write the first entry
Tell your spouse: “Thank you for tending this altar fire with me.”
lessons.noon: “Fire shall be kept burning on the altar continually; it shall not go out” — Holy Spirit, right now add wood and kindle the fire in my heart.

mem.t: Again, assuredly I tell you, that if two of you will agree on earth concerning anything that they will ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.

s: Take a twenty-minute walk around your neighborhood, praying short prayers for the people and places you pass: neighbors, schools, shops, churches.
Find somewhere to sit down and swap your “three prayer requests” with each other.
Holding hands, each of you prays one sentence for the other; then pray the Lord's Prayer together.
When you get home, write the first page of your prayer journal.

lessons.title: The Promise of Agreement
lessons.theme: When two pray in agreement, the Father hears

v: Again, assuredly I tell you, that if two of you will agree on earth concerning anything that they will ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them.”

lessons.still: If you can, take your spouse's hand right now; if you are alone, place your hand over your heart. Be still for a moment and remember Jesus' promise: where two or three gather in his name, he is there among them.
lessons.light: 321 Light: When couples find it hard to pray together, it's often not because they don't know how, but because self is on the throne: we don't want to look weak in front of each other, or we are still angry inside. Agreement begins with being self-emptied. When both of us lay ourselves down and turn to Jesus, our prayers stop being two separate monologues and become one symphony.
lessons.jesus: On his most agonizing night, in Gethsemane, Jesus took three disciples with him and said, “Stay here and watch with me” (Matthew 26:38). The Son of God himself longed for others to pray with him. Jesus shows us that inviting others to pray with us is not weakness; it is an expression of faith.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for promising to hear two people who pray in agreement. We confess that sometimes we don't want to pray together because of pride, busyness, or distance between our hearts. Please remove every obstacle and make our prayers sound together like music in harmony. Lord Jesus, be always in our midst. Amen.
teach: Jesus said, “if two of you will agree on earth concerning anything that they will ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:19). The Greek word for “agree” shares a root with our word “symphony”: it means to sound together in harmony. Picture two instruments with different tones playing from the same score. When a husband and wife pray in agreement, two different people lift their voices together according to God's heart.

This promise is not a way to control God through prayer; it is an invitation into God's will. To agree with each other, we must first agree with God. So when couples pray together, they often find their own thinking being adjusted: they started out asking only for the problem to go away, and end up asking God to change them. Prayer doesn't just change circumstances; it changes the people who pray.

Jesus went on: “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them” (Matthew 18:20). The smallest gathering is two people. When a couple prays in their living room, the Lord himself is present. As you pray together, Jesus is not a spectator; he is the Lord in your midst. A couple praying as one is the most powerful, yet most often neglected, spiritual resource in a home.
q: What is my biggest hesitation about praying together with my spouse?
Do I mostly ask God to change my circumstances or my spouse, or do I also ask him to change me?
talk: When we pray together, what feels most comfortable for you, and what feels least comfortable?
This month, what is the one thing we most want to entrust to God together, in agreement?
acts: Hold hands today and pray together for one minute
Each name one thing you want to entrust to God together this month
Make Matthew 18:19 your phone wallpaper
lessons.noon: “there I am in the middle of them” — Lord Jesus, be here in our midst right now.

lessons.title: Start with One Sentence
lessons.theme: The Lord's Prayer is the best starting point for praying together

v: When he finished praying in a certain place, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John also taught his disciples.”
He said to them, “When you pray, say, ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. May your Kingdom come. May your will be done on earth, as it is in heaven.
Give us day by day our daily bread.
Forgive us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone who is indebted to us. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’”

lessons.still: Be still. You don't need to find beautiful words. Like a child talking to a father, simply say one sentence to God: “Father, here I am.” That is how prayer begins.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Sometimes we are afraid to pray in front of our spouse because we fear being compared or not saying it well, and that, too, is self at work. Prayer is not a performance; it is a child talking to the Father. When our focus is on Jesus rather than on how well we speak, we are set free.
lessons.jesus: At the tomb of Lazarus, Jesus lifted up his eyes and said just one sentence: “Father, I thank you that you listened to me” (John 11:41). It was a very short prayer, followed by the miracle of a dead man raised to life. Jesus shows us that the power of prayer lies not in its length, but in intimate trust in the Father.
lessons.pray: Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy; may your Kingdom come in our home. Give us day by day our daily bread. Forgive us our sins, for we also forgive each other. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. Amen.
teach: When the disciples saw Jesus praying, they asked him, “Lord, teach us to pray” (Luke 11:1). Even disciples who walked with Jesus every day needed to learn how to pray, so it is perfectly normal if we feel we don't know how, or feel shy about praying out loud in front of our spouse. The good news is that Jesus didn't hand them a thick prayer manual; he gave them a short prayer.

The Lord's Prayer can become the framework for a couple's prayers: first we honor God as great, that his name be kept holy; then we seek his will, that his Kingdom come; then we ask for our daily needs; next we ask for forgiveness and forgive others; and finally we ask for protection from temptation and from the evil one. Notice that the Lord's Prayer says “us” and “our”, never “I” or “me”. It was a prayer of togetherness from the start.

Couples can begin praying together with a single sentence. Think of learning to swim: you don't need to swim a hundred meters on day one; just put your feet in the water. Take turns saying one sentence each, one thank-you or one request, or slowly pray the Lord's Prayer together. If one of you is more used to praying, slow down and keep it short so the other doesn't feel pressured. The value of praying together isn't in how long the words are, but in two hearts turning to the Father together.
q: When I pray in front of others, what worries me most? Does that worry need to be released before God?
Which line of the Lord's Prayer do I need most right now?
talk: Let's try it: each of us says just one sentence of prayer. Would you like to start with a thank-you or a request?
When is it easiest for us to pray one sentence together: before leaving in the morning, at meals, or before bed?
acts: Slowly pray the Lord's Prayer together today
Before bed, each say one sentence of prayer
Choose a set time each day to pray together
lessons.noon: “Lord, teach us to pray” — Lord, right now I want to speak one sentence to you, like a child.

lessons.title: Praying for Your Spouse
lessons.theme: Intercession is the deepest love and the quietest protection

v: For this cause, we also, since the day we heard this, don’t cease praying and making requests for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding,
that you may walk worthily of the Lord, to please him in all respects, bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God,
Moreover, as for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you; but I will instruct you in the good and the right way.

lessons.still: Picture your spouse's face, and think of the pressures they may be facing today. Don't rush to ask for anything. First, quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you for entrusting this person to me. I will keep watch over them in prayer.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Complaining about my spouse puts the focus on their problems; praying for my spouse turns the focus to Jesus. It is the Holy Spirit who changes hearts, not my nagging. When I stop trying to play the Holy Spirit in my spouse's life and start praying for them, I myself move from the self-ruled life toward the self-emptied life.
lessons.jesus: On the night he was betrayed, Jesus prayed for his disciples: “I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one” (John 17:15). He knew the temptations they would face and interceded for them specifically. Jesus still intercedes for us today; he is our example in praying for our spouse.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for giving us to each other. Help us never to cease praying for one another, asking not only for outward success, but that each of us may be filled with the knowledge of your will and grow in knowing you. While we wait, strengthen our faith and change us as well. Amen.
teach: Samuel told the Israelites, “far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you” (1 Samuel 12:23). In Samuel's eyes, to stop praying for people was a sin, because intercession is a duty of love. In marriage, no one knows our spouse's weaknesses and needs better than we do, so no one is better placed to pray for them.

Paul told the Colossian believers that he and his companions “don't cease praying and making requests for you” (Colossians 1:9). He asked not merely for outward success but for spiritual growth: that they “may be filled with the knowledge of his will”, that they “may walk worthily of the Lord”, “bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God” (Colossians 1:9–10). We can pray for our spouse the same way: beyond their work and health, we can ask God to help them know him, experience him, and bear fruit.

Genesis records, “Isaac entreated the LORD for his wife, because she was barren” (Genesis 25:21), and they waited twenty years. When we intercede, God sometimes answers by granting our request, sometimes by asking us to wait, and sometimes by changing us while we wait. A couple's prayer list is a good tool: each of you writes down three things you'd like the other to pray for, swap lists, pray for each other every day, and watch for what God does.
q: Which do I spend more time doing: praying for my spouse, or complaining to them and reminding them?
Beyond outward needs, what spiritual blessing do I most want God to bring about in my spouse's life?
talk: Each of us names three things we'd like the other to pray for; let's write them down and swap.
In what area do you especially need me to keep watch over you in prayer right now? (If your spouse can't join you at the moment, write down three things you want to pray for them.)
acts: Swap your “three prayer requests” lists
Pray for your spouse today at a set time
Text your spouse: “I just prayed for you.”
lessons.noon: “far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you” — Lord, right now I place my spouse in your hands and keep watch over them in prayer.

lessons.title: Turning Worries into Shared Prayer
lessons.theme: Clear away what hinders prayer, and find peace in praying together

v: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.
Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.

lessons.still: Bring your worries to mind one by one: family, work, health, money, or a knot between the two of you that hasn't been untied. Don't rush to fix them. Just place them, one at a time, into the Lord's hands.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Worry is often rooted in my wanting to control the outcome myself. Prayer hands control back to God: let people be people, and let God be God. When a couple hands their worries over together, they move from pressuring each other to trusting God together, and God's peace guards our hearts.
lessons.jesus: Jesus' ministry was extremely busy, yet “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there” (Mark 1:35). The busier he was, the more he put communion with the Father first. Jesus shows us that prayer is not something we do after the busyness is over; it is the source of strength for facing it.
lessons.pray: Lord of peace, we tell you all the worries in our hearts. Wherever there are knots between us, help us confess to each other and forgive each other; whatever hinders us from praying as one, please take it away. May your peace, which surpasses all understanding, guard our hearts and our thoughts. Amen.
teach: Paul says, “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6). Many couples make their worries the topic of conversation, grow more anxious the more they talk, and end up arguing. But when the same worries become the content of shared prayer, they turn from burdens we load onto each other into concerns we hand over to God. Picture two people lifting a heavy stone onto a cart together, then handing it to the One who is strong enough to push it.

The most common obstacle to praying together is a knot in the heart. James says, “Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed” (James 5:16). Peter also urges husbands to honor their wives, “that your prayers may not be hindered” (1 Peter 3:7). When there is anger or something hidden in our hearts, prayer gets stuck. A simple “I'm sorry, I spoke too harshly just now” is often where praying as one begins.

Other obstacles are very practical: being too busy, too tired, feeling awkward, being at different places spiritually, or one spouse being unwilling for now. We can face them one at a time. If you're busy, keep it short; if you're tired, say one sentence before bed; if it feels awkward, start by reading Scripture aloud together; if you're at different paces, be patient with each other; if your spouse isn't willing, start by praying for them yourself. Paul promises, “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:7).
q: What is our family's biggest worry right now? Am I turning it into complaining or into prayer?
Is there a “knot” between my spouse and me that needs to be untied before we can truly pray as one?
talk: What do you think is the biggest obstacle to our praying together? How can we break through it together?
Right now, each of us names one worry, and then we each pray one sentence for the other's worry.
acts: Write down one worry and pray about it together
If there's a knot between you, start by telling your spouse “I'm sorry”
Before bed, say together: “Lord, we give tomorrow to you.”
lessons.noon: “In nothing be anxious” — Lord, right now I trade my worries for prayer and thanksgiving.

lessons.title: Recording What God Has Done
lessons.theme: A couple's prayer journal helps us see God's faithfulness

v: Peter therefore was kept in the prison, but constant prayer was made by the assembly to God for him.
Thinking about that, he came to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was called Mark, where many were gathered together and were praying.
Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving,

lessons.still: Think back over the past year. What have you prayed about together? Which prayers have been answered, and which are still waiting? Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you that you heard every one.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: We easily remember our problems but forget God's grace; that is seeing things from a human point of view. Recording what God has done is practice in seeing our home from God's point of view. Every check mark testifies that Jesus reigns in our home and receives all the glory.
lessons.jesus: Jesus told a parable “that they must always pray and not give up” (Luke 18:1). He knew prayer would involve waiting, and that people easily lose heart, so he told the story of the widow who kept pleading for justice to encourage us to keep asking. Jesus shows us that persevering in prayer is itself a lesson in faith.
lessons.pray: Faithful God, thank you for hearing our prayers, and thank you for being with us while we wait. Help us to continue steadfastly in prayer, watching with thanksgiving, not giving up and not forgetting. May our home be a house of prayer, so that others see your faithfulness and you receive all the glory. Amen.
teach: Peter was locked in prison, his life in danger, “but constant prayer was made by the assembly to God for him” (Acts 12:5); the church kept praying. After the angel led him out of prison, he went to the house of Mary, “where many were gathered together and were praying” (Acts 12:12). A home became a place of prayer, and a witness to a miracle. When a couple prays as one, our home can become that kind of place too.

Interestingly, when Peter knocked at the door, the people inside at first didn't believe their prayer had been answered. We are often the same: we pray, but forget to watch for God's answer. That is why Paul says, “Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving” (Colossians 4:2). “Watching” means paying attention to what God is doing; “thanksgiving” means remembering what God has done. A couple's prayer journal is a tool that helps us keep watching with thanksgiving.

Get a simple notebook and divide it into three columns: date, prayer request, and God's answer. Look through it during your weekly family worship, check off the prayers that have been answered, and keep praying for those still waiting. Looking back over this week: the promise of agreement, starting with one sentence, praying for your spouse, clearing away obstacles, and recording what God has done. One day this little notebook will be your family's most precious testimony of faith.
q: Is there a prayer God has already answered that I forgot to thank him for?
What have I been praying about for a long time and am starting to lose heart over? Am I willing to keep entrusting it to him?
talk: Together, recall one time God answered prayer in our marriage, and share how each of us felt back then.
How will we use our prayer journal? Who will write in it? When will we look back over it together?
acts: Get a notebook for “Our Prayer Journal”
Write down three answered prayers and give thanks together
Agree to look back over your prayer list together once a week
lessons.noon: “Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving” — Lord, right now I thank you that you have always heard our prayers.

47.title: Parenting as One: Training Children in the Way They Should Go

mem.t: Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.

date.t: What Our Family Will Pass On
s: Each of you share: growing up, what was the most precious thing a parent or older relative left you? It doesn't have to be an object; it could be a saying or a habit.

Together, write down three values you hope the next generation will carry away from your home. The next generation could be your own children, or nieces and nephews, Sunday school kids, or spiritual sons and daughters.
Write a small blessing card for a child you both care about, with their name and a Bible verse, and find a chance to give it to them or keep it for them.
Holding hands, read Proverbs 22:6 together and pray as one for this child.

lessons.title: On Our Hearts First
lessons.theme: Parenting begins with parents loving God with all their heart

v: You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart;
and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.

lessons.still: Be still. For now, don't think about your children or anyone else's; think only about yourself and God. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, before I teach anyone else, be the one I love most in my heart.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Parenting easily slides into the self-ruled life: we want our children to make us look good or to fulfill the dreams we never reached. Change starts with me: when I first let Jesus reign in my heart, what my children see is not parents making demands of them, but a couple being changed by God.
lessons.jesus: When someone asked Jesus which commandment was the greatest, he quoted this very passage from Deuteronomy: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matthew 22:37). Jesus loved the Father this way his whole life, so everything he taught, he lived out first.
lessons.pray: Father, we confess that we are often in a hurry to teach others without first loving you with all our heart. Engrave your words on our hearts first, so that at home, on the road, when we lie down and when we rise up, we naturally speak of you. And let the children around us see a real you in our lives. Amen.
teach: On every flight, the cabin crew reminds us: if the oxygen masks drop, put on your own mask first, then help the child next to you. That isn't selfishness; it's order. Deuteronomy 6 is about raising children, yet its first word is not “teach your children” but “You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:5). Parents need to breathe in oxygen themselves before they have anything to give the next generation.

Then God says, “These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart” (Deuteronomy 6:6), and only then, “you shall teach them diligently to your children” (Deuteronomy 6:7). The order is clear: first in the heart, then on the lips. The Hebrew word behind “teach them diligently” carries the sense of sharpening something again and again, like honing a knife, engraving it stroke after stroke. Parenting is not one big lecture; it is repetition, day after day.

God also shows us where this teaching happens: you “shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up” (Deuteronomy 6:7). Faith doesn't only show up on Sundays or at family devotions; it shows up in everyday conversations at the dinner table, in the car, at bedtime, and in the morning. Families with children can live this way; couples without children can apply this passage just as much to nieces and nephews, the neighbors' kids, or the little ones in Sunday school.
q: Right now, is God truly in the place of “first love” in my heart? Or is it my children, my work, or other people's opinions?
What parts of the faith I want the next generation to learn am I not yet truly living out myself?
talk: In our everyday routine (meals, driving, bedtime), which moment is best for talking about God naturally?
Growing up, do you remember hearing about faith while “sitting in the house” or “walking by the way”? (If your spouse can't join you at the moment, write down your own memory.)
acts: Today, first spend five minutes reading a passage just for yourself
Choose an everyday moment to say a natural word of thanks to God
Pray for a child in your life by name
lessons.noon: “These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart” — Lord, engrave your words on my heart right now.

lessons.title: One Voice
lessons.theme: When parents are united, children feel secure

v: Did he not make you one, although he had the residue of the Spirit? Why one? He sought godly offspring. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let no one deal treacherously against the wife of his youth.
make my joy full by being like-minded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind;

lessons.still: Think of the last time the two of you disagreed in front of your children or younger relatives. Don't rush to judge who was right. Simply tell the Lord: “Lord, I am willing to be united with my spouse first, before I try to teach anyone else.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Arguing in front of the children over who is right is pride provoking pride, and the children become the battlefield. When the humbler one says first, “Let's talk about this in our room,” that is letting Jesus reign. Parental unity isn't about who wins; it's about standing together under God's standard.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Everything he said and did was in complete harmony with the Father; he never contradicted the Father in front of others. Precisely because the Father and the Son are one, the disciples could know God clearly. Jesus' oneness with the Father is our example for parenting as one.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for making us one and entrusting the next generation to us. Forgive us for undermining each other and talking past each other in front of our children. Help us to unite privately first and then speak together, so that our home becomes a safe harbor for the next generation and soil where godliness is passed on. Amen.
teach: Picture a small boat with two people rowing at the back, one paddling left and the other paddling right. The boat just spins in circles, and the children on board get seasick. What children need most is often not the perfect parenting method, but parents speaking with one voice, heading in one direction. When parents undermine each other, children learn to slip through the cracks: if Dad says no, ask Mom; if Mom says no, go find Dad. Over time, they lose their sense of security.

Malachi says God made husband and wife one, and asks, “Why one? He sought godly offspring” (Malachi 2:15). One of God's purposes for marriage is for godliness to be passed down from generation to generation. A couple's unity isn't only about the two of them; it is the soil in which the next generation's faith grows. That is why the verse continues, “Therefore take heed to your spirit” (Malachi 2:15). Guarding our marriage is guarding the next generation.

Paul urged the church to be “like-minded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind” (Philippians 2:2). Being united doesn't mean two people think exactly alike; it means being willing to talk things through privately first, and then speak to the children together. One practical rule: don't contradict each other in front of the children. When you disagree, say, “Let us talk it over, and then we'll let you know.” That sentence tells children: Mom and Dad are on the same team.
q: Have I ever contradicted my spouse in front of our children or younger relatives? What was I really wanting at that moment?
In parenting or in how I treat others, which of my firm positions is really about my self rather than God's standard?
talk: In disciplining our children (or dealing with younger relatives), what do we disagree about most often? Can we agree on a way to “talk it over privately first”?
Tell your spouse one thing you appreciate about how they parent or care for younger people.
acts: Agree with your spouse on a code phrase: “Let's talk it over”
Today, affirm your spouse once in front of your children or younger relatives
Write down one parenting matter this week that you will discuss together before deciding
lessons.noon: “being of one accord, of one mind” — Lord, right now make me one in heart with my spouse.

lessons.title: Discipline Without Provoking
lessons.theme: Discipline is for the child's good, not for venting the parent's anger

v: You fathers, don’t provoke your children to wrath, but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
For they indeed for a few days disciplined us as seemed good to them, but he for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness.
All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.

lessons.still: Recall a time you spoke harshly to a child or younger person. What did you really care about in that moment: their good, or saving face? Quietly hand that moment to the Lord, and let his gentleness reach you first.
lessons.light: 321 Light: We “provoke our children to wrath” often because we parents are angry ourselves: we feel offended, embarrassed, or out of control. That is self on the throne. Self-emptied discipline deals with my own emotions first, and then with the child's behavior. Let people be people, and let God be God; never use a child as a tool to prove myself.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus corrected Martha, who was busy and complaining, he didn't scold or shame her; he gently called her name: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things” (Luke 10:41). He named the problem, yet she could feel that she was loved. Jesus shows us that correction can be both clear and gentle.
lessons.pray: Father of spirits, thank you that you discipline us for our good, so that we may share in your holiness. Forgive us for the times we disciplined our children according to our own moods and wounded their hearts. Heal the wounds we carried from the generation before us, and make our discipline gentle and firm, bearing the fruit of peace. Amen.
teach: A gardener prunes a rose so that it will bloom more fully; but if someone hacks at it with shears to vent their anger, the rose is wounded and withers. Discipline works the same way. Paul says, “You fathers, don't provoke your children to wrath, but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4). In a culture where fathers held enormous authority, this was a revolutionary statement: authority is for nurturing, not for crushing.

Hebrews compares two kinds of discipline: earthly fathers “disciplined us as seemed good to them”, but God disciplines us “for our profit” (Hebrews 12:10). Our discipline is often “as seemed good to us”: extra strict when we're in a bad mood, lax when we're tired. Good discipline asks: will this actually benefit my child's life? Rules should be clear and consistent; our tone should be gentle and firm.

We need to say this very clearly: hitting or yelling to vent, humiliating or belittling, intimidating or threatening are not what the Bible calls discipline; they are harm. If anyone in your home is suffering physical, verbal, or emotional violence, safety always comes first; please seek help from a pastor and from professionals. God's discipline “afterward... yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11). True discipline bears the fruit of peace, not fear.
q: When I discipline or correct someone, is it mostly for their good, or to vent my own anger?
Which part of the way I was disciplined in my family of origin needs the Lord's healing?
talk: Is there a rule in our home (or in how we treat younger relatives) that we need to restate clearly together and enforce consistently as a pair?
When my emotions flare up, what “pause signal” would you like us to have, so I can calm down before I speak?
acts: Today, before correcting anyone, take three deep breaths before you speak
If you have spoken harshly to a child or younger person, go and say sorry today
Write down one house rule that the two of you will enforce consistently
lessons.noon: “nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” — Lord, right now let my words carry your gentleness.

lessons.title: Children Grow Up Watching Us
lessons.theme: Example teaches deeper than words; faith is lived out and passed on

v: having been reminded of the sincere faith that is in you, which lived first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and, I am persuaded, in you also.
But you remain in the things which you have learned and have been assured of, knowing from whom you have learned them.
From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Imagine a pair of little eyes watching how you speak today, how you treat your spouse, how you handle pressure. No need to be nervous; just quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, make me someone worth imitating.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Teaching by words comes from the head; teaching by example comes from the heart. Living from the head leads to worry, and the more we lecture, the more worn out we get; when we live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by ourselves, life flows out naturally. Change works from the inside out: first my life is changed, then my way of living, and only then my relationships and the next generation.
lessons.jesus: After washing his disciples' feet, Jesus said, “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you” (John 13:15). He didn't begin with a lecture on humility; he first bent down to serve. Jesus' teaching began with his example.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for giving us an example yourself. Make our lives a gospel the next generation can see: respecting each other in front of them, humbly admitting our faults when we're wrong, and praying together in hard times. Remember the places in our home where we are not yet one in faith, and let our sincere faith be passed on from generation to generation. Amen.
teach: When children learn to talk, they don't learn from a dictionary; they pick up their parents' accent. Our tone of voice, the way we get angry, how we react to difficulty, all quietly become the next generation's “accent.” Paul wrote to Timothy that his faith “lived first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice” (2 Timothy 1:5). Faith is lived out and passed down from one generation to the next.

It's worth noting that Timothy's father was Greek, and the Bible never mentions him believing. In other words, in a home where faith was not shared, a grandmother and a mother still passed genuine faith on to Timothy through their lives. If you are the only believer in your home, don't lose heart: God sees your prayers and your example, and he will use them. The seeds of faith often sprout quietly where no one can see.

Paul goes on: you know “from whom you have learned them. From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures” (2 Timothy 3:14–15). What Timothy remembered was not just the verses, but the people who taught them to him. Children may not remember every lesson we teach, but they will certainly remember how we loved our spouse, how we admitted our mistakes, and how we prayed in hard times. The best curriculum is a marriage in which the parents love each other.
q: If the children around me copied exactly how I treated my spouse this week, would I feel glad or uneasy?
What kind of life do I hope the next generation will remember me for?
talk: What good habit do you see in me that you'd like our children (or younger relatives) to learn?
What could we model together in front of children or younger people? For example, apologizing, praying, or giving thanks.
acts: Today, thank your spouse in front of your children or younger relatives
When you get something wrong, say it face to face: “I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
Tell a child how you came to know God when you were young
lessons.noon: “the sincere faith that is in you” — Lord, right now let my faith be sincere and real.

lessons.title: Let the Little Children Come
lessons.theme: Every couple can raise spiritual sons and daughters

v: They were bringing to him little children, that he should touch them, but the disciples rebuked those who were bringing them.
But when Jesus saw it, he was moved with indignation and said to them, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these.
Most certainly I tell you, whoever will not receive God’s Kingdom like a little child, he will in no way enter into it.”
He took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.
Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.

lessons.still: Think back over this week. Which child or young person has God placed on your heart? It may be your own child, or a niece or nephew, a neighbor, a child at church. Quietly bring their name before the Lord.
lessons.light: 321 Light: From a human point of view, whether we have children and whether they succeed often becomes the yardstick for a family. From God's point of view, what matters is whether we bring people to Jesus. Building a household that belongs to God isn't about how many people are in it, but about whether life is being multiplied.
lessons.jesus: When the disciples argued about who was the greatest, Jesus had a little child stand among them and said, “Whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me” (Matthew 18:5). Jesus treats welcoming a child as welcoming himself. Every time we welcome a child, we are welcoming the Lord.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for opening your arms to every child. Whether or not we have children of our own, make our home a place where children are welcomed and blessed. We are willing to pray for and walk alongside the next generation you have entrusted to us, so that they go in the way they should go and do not depart from it when they are old. Amen.
teach: The disciples thought Jesus was too busy, so they turned away the people bringing children to him. When Jesus saw it, “he was moved with indignation and said to them, ‘Allow the little children to come to me! Don't forbid them’” (Mark 10:14). Then “He took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them” (Mark 10:16). Jesus didn't ask whose children they were; he simply opened his arms and welcomed them. This scene tells us that every child deserves to be brought to Jesus.

Some couples don't have children. Perhaps they have longed for them for years, or perhaps life has unfolded differently. In God's eyes your home lacks nothing; your marriage is just as complete and just as precious. Paul never had children of his own, yet he wrote, “My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19). Spiritual parenthood is a calling every couple can receive.

So Proverbs says, “Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it” (Proverbs 22:6). “The way he should go” can be understood as the path God has set for that particular child. Parenting means helping children know God and walk the road he has prepared for them, not making copies of ourselves. Whether they are children by birth, by adoption, or spiritual children, we are only God's stewards, walking with them for a stretch of the road toward Jesus.
q: Who are the “children” God has placed in my life? Have I, like the disciples, ever turned them away because I was busy?
Which part of my idea of a “complete family” needs to shift from a human point of view to God's point of view?
talk: Of this week's lessons, which sentence most reminded you of how we can walk alongside the next generation?
Could we choose one child or young person together to pray for regularly and care for over this coming year?
acts: Name a child and lay hands on them or pray a blessing over them
Give a child in your life one specific word of affirmation
Choose with your spouse one child you will pray for regularly this year
lessons.noon: “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them” — Lord Jesus, right now I bring this child to you.

48.title: Our Home, a Lampstand for the Gospel

mem.t: Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

date.t: Lighting the Lamp in Our Home
s: Together, write down three families or friends you care about who don't yet know the Lord, and each share why they came to mind.
Choose one family from your list and set a date to invite them over for a meal or an outing. It doesn't need to be lavish, just sincere.
Think together of one small detail that will make your guests feel welcome: a cup of hot tea, a little card with their name on it, a dish they love.
Light a candle or switch on a small lamp, hold hands, and pray for each family on your list by name; then read Matthew 5:16 together.

lessons.title: A Lamp Belongs on a Stand
lessons.theme: A home's light isn't meant to be hidden; it's meant to shine on others

v: You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.
Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house.
Even so, let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

lessons.still: If you can, turn off the main light in the room and leave just one small lamp on. Look at that little light and quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, could our home become a lamp like this?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: If our good works are meant to win praise for our family, that is the self-ruled life; if they are meant to help people see the Father, that is letting Jesus receive all the glory. The focus of light is not the lamp, but the people it shines on, and the One who lit it.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness” (John 8:12). He walked into tax collectors' homes, to the bedsides of the sick, onto fishermen's boats, and wherever he went, light shone. Our light is borrowed from him; as long as we follow him closely, our home will shine.
lessons.pray: Jesus, Light of the world, thank you for lighting up our home. We confess that we often hide our lamp under a basket and just want to live our own lives. Let our love for each other, our making up, and our kindness be seen, so that those who see them give glory to the Father in heaven, not to us. Amen.
teach: On a night when the power goes out and the whole street is pitch dark, if just one household lights a candle, that window becomes the warmest place on the street. Jesus said, “You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can't be hidden” (Matthew 5:14). He didn't say, “Try hard to become light”; he said, “You are.” Those who belong to Christ carry light within them.

Jesus went on with an everyday picture: “Neither do you light a lamp and put it under a measuring basket, but on a stand; and it shines to all who are in the house” (Matthew 5:15). Most Jewish homes of that time had only one room, so one lamp set on a stand lit up the whole household. Today many Christian families are like a lamp under a basket: we look after ourselves, don't want the hassle, and don't want to be noticed. But a lamp's whole purpose is to give light.

How does this light shine out? Jesus said, “let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). Neighbors and relatives may never come to hear a sermon, but they will see how we as a couple talk to each other, how we make up after an argument, how we help people in need. Home is the most authentic pulpit, and a couple's love for each other is a sermon people can see; and the glory goes to the Father in heaven, not to us.
q: Is our home right now more like a lamp “on a stand” or one “under a basket”? What makes me want to hide the light?
When I do good, do I care more about people seeing me, or seeing the Father?
talk: What kind of light do our neighbors and relatives see in our home? Which part do you think most needs God to polish it?
Is there a habit in our home that has already been quietly helping others see God?
acts: Today, take the initiative to greet a neighbor or coworker
Light a small lamp at home as a reminder that you are the light of the world
Write down one small thing you can do for a neighbor this week
lessons.noon: “You are the light of the world” — Lord Jesus, right now let your light shine out through me.

lessons.title: An Open Door
lessons.theme: Hospitality isn't showing off our home; it's sharing our life

v: And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.
Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.
As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.
Don’t forget to show hospitality to strangers, for in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it.

lessons.still: Picture your front door. When was the last time someone walked through it and shared a meal or a cup of tea in your home? Quietly ask the Lord to open your heart wider, and your door as well.
lessons.light: 321 Light: When we hold back from hospitality, it is often because we fear our imperfections will be seen, and that is a hidden pride; when we grumble while hosting, it is self on the throne, keeping score of what we give. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things: guests won't remember whether the floor was spotless, but they will remember whether they were loved.
lessons.jesus: Levi threw a great banquet for Jesus at his house, and many tax collectors and others sat at the table with him. The religious leaders grumbled, but Jesus said, “Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick do” (Luke 5:31). Jesus was glad to sit at sinners' tables. He shows us that the dinner table is the most natural place for the gospel.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for welcoming us first and giving us a place in your house. Forgive us for closing our door and thinking only of ourselves. Make us one in heart, sharing the work according to our gifts, glad to be hospitable without grumbling, so that everyone who walks into our home experiences your love. Amen.
teach: Many people are reluctant to invite others over because they feel their home isn't big enough, tidy enough, or their cooking isn't good enough. But hospitality is different from entertaining. Entertaining thinks about “me” and wants to impress; hospitality thinks about “you” and wants people to feel loved. Abraham was sitting at his tent door in the heat of the day, and as soon as he saw travelers passing by he ran to meet them: “let a little water be fetched, wash your feet” (Genesis 18:4). A basin of water and a piece of bread: that is hospitality.

Peter says, “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling” (1 Peter 4:9). The Greek word for hospitality literally means “love of strangers.” Peter places it right after “above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves” (1 Peter 4:8), and right before “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another” (1 Peter 4:10). Hospitality is not an extra burden; it is love taking concrete shape. And no one has to carry it alone: a husband and wife can share the work according to their gifts.

Hebrews says, “Don't forget to show hospitality to strangers, for in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it” (Hebrews 13:2). Our dinner table may be the only place all week where a lonely person is asked how they are doing, or the first place an unbelieving friend experiences God's love. When a couple opens their door together, their home becomes the front porch of the gospel.
q: What is the real reason I'm hesitant or unwilling to welcome people into our home? Fear of the hassle, of being seen, or of the cost?
Through whose home, whose dinner table, has God let me experience his love?
talk: When it comes to hospitality, what gifts do you think each of us has? How can we share the work so neither of us gets too worn out?
If we were to invite one person or family over this month, who comes to mind first?
acts: Set a date with your spouse to invite someone over
Today, send a message to check in on someone who is lonely
Clear a corner of your home that is always ready for guests
lessons.noon: “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling” — Lord, right now open my heart wider, and my door as well.

lessons.title: The Home of Priscilla and Aquila
lessons.theme: When husband and wife work together, their home becomes an extension of the church

v: Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by race, an eloquent man, came to Ephesus. He was mighty in the Scriptures.
This man had been instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, although he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately.
Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus,
who risked their own necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks, but also all the assemblies of the Gentiles.
Greet the assembly that is in their house. Greet Epaenetus, my beloved, who is the first fruits of Achaia to Christ.

lessons.still: Think of something the two of you have done together to serve God, however small. Quietly thank the Lord, because he calls not only individuals but also couples to serve together.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Priscilla and Aquila were first a couple united in heart, and only then a couple united in ministry. If a couple is not one at home, their ministry outside will struggle to last; when we first let Jesus reign in our home, ministry flows naturally out from it.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus sent out his disciples, he “sent them two by two ahead of him” (Luke 10:1). He knew that on the road of service, two are better than one: they support and remind each other. A husband and wife serving together fits perfectly with the way Jesus sends people out.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for using the ordinary home of Priscilla and Aquila. Make us, too, one in heart and one in your work, each fitting in with the other according to our gifts. Open the door of our home to people in need, help us welcome and build others up with gentle hearts, and let our home become a small outpost of your Kingdom. Amen.
teach: There is a couple in the New Testament whose names appear six times, and every time they appear together: Priscilla and Aquila. They were tentmakers, and when Paul came to Corinth, “he lived with them and worked” (Acts 18:3). They had no pulpit, only a workshop and a home, yet they became some of Paul's most important coworkers. The homes God uses are often ordinary, but open.

One day the gifted speaker Apollos was preaching in the synagogue, but his understanding of the gospel was still incomplete. “But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately” (Acts 18:26). Notice that they didn't correct him in public or embarrass him; they “took him aside,” very likely into their home, and gently filled in what was missing. One couple's dinner table helped shape a man who would become an important preacher.

Paul later wrote, “Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus” (Romans 16:3), and added, “Greet the assembly that is in their house” (Romans 16:5): the church met in their home. (Prisca is a short form of Priscilla.) Wherever they moved, their home became a place where believers gathered. This doesn't mean every home must start a church; it reminds us that husbands and wives can serve together, and a Christian home is itself a small outpost of the gospel.
q: Am I more used to serving on my own, or with my spouse? What has kept us from serving together more often?
What does the gentleness of Priscilla and Aquila, who “took him aside,” teach me about how I correct others?
talk: When we team up, what do you think we're best at for blessing others? For example, one of us cooks and the other listens.
In the coming year, what small act of service could we do together? (If your spouse can't join you at the moment, write down one step you could start with on your own.)
acts: Name one gift your spouse has that is wonderful in serving
Pray together for one minute for your small group or church
Write down one act of service you could do as a couple
lessons.noon: “my fellow workers in Christ Jesus” — Lord, right now make us, as a couple, your fellow workers.

lessons.title: Go Home and Tell Your People
lessons.theme: Witness begins with those closest to us, with our lives and with gentle words

v: As he was entering into the boat, he who had been possessed by demons begged him that he might be with him.
He didn’t allow him, but said to him, “Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you and how he had mercy on you.”
He went his way, and began to proclaim in Decapolis how Jesus had done great things for him, and everyone marveled.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear,

lessons.still: Think of a relative in your extended family who doesn't yet know the Lord, and quietly speak their name before him. Don't rush to work out what to say; just ask the Lord to give you a heart of love for them first.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The biggest obstacle to sharing the gospel with family is often the urge to win: we're eager to prove we're right and they're wrong. That is pride pitted against pride. Live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by yourself; when our focus is on Jesus rather than on winning the argument, our family can see him.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus met the Samaritan woman at the well, his first words were not a rebuke but a request: “Give me a drink” (John 4:7). He crossed the barriers of ethnicity and gender first, humbling himself to speak to her. Jesus shows us that gospel conversations often begin with a humble request and genuine care.
lessons.pray: Merciful Lord, thank you for the great things you have done for our home. Give us hearts of love for our families, help us live out our hope in front of them, and when they ask, help us answer with humility and reverence. We place our relatives who don't yet believe into your hands; please draw them to yourself. Amen.
teach: The man Jesus set free from a legion of demons wanted to follow Jesus. But Jesus didn't allow it. He told him, “Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you and how he had mercy on you” (Mark 5:19). Jesus gave him his first mission field not in some faraway place, but in his own home and among his own people. For many of us, sharing the gospel with strangers is easy; opening our mouths with family is the hardest of all.

Our families know our weaknesses best, so when we witness to them, the most powerful thing is not argument, but change. Jesus told the man to share two things: what great things the Lord had done for him, and how the Lord had mercy on him. We don't need to memorize a script; we just need to tell honestly what has changed in our marriage, our temper, and our family since we came to faith. A home that has been reconciled is the best testimony there is.

Peter says, “Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear” (1 Peter 3:15). Notice: “everyone who asks.” First we live out our hope so that people become curious, and then we answer gently. If your spouse doesn't yet believe, Peter also reminds us that through our conduct they “may be won” (1 Peter 3:1). No pressure, no nagging, just ongoing love and prayer, leaving the outcome to God.
q: Toward the relative I find hardest to talk to, is there more love in my heart, or more of a desire to persuade them?
If someone asked me, “What difference has faith made for you?”, could I name one real, specific change?
talk: Since we came to faith, what do you think is the greatest thing God has done in our home?
Which relative in our extended family could we begin with simply by caring and being present, without rushing to preach?
acts: Write two sentences of testimony about what the Lord has done for your family
Today, call a relative who doesn't yet believe, just to say hello
Pray for a family member who doesn't yet believe, by name
lessons.noon: “tell them what great things the Lord has done for you” — Lord, right now help me remember the great things you have done for me.

lessons.title: Today Salvation Has Come to This House
lessons.theme: When one person is changed by Jesus, the whole household is blessed

v: When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him, and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.”
He hurried, came down, and received him joyfully.
When they saw it, they all murmured, saying, “He has gone in to lodge with a man who is a sinner.”
Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.”
Jesus said to him, “Today, salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham.

lessons.still: Imagine Jesus coming to your front door today, looking up, calling your name, and saying, “Today I must stay at your house.” What is your first reaction? Quietly, and joyfully, open the door to him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: When our life changes, our way of living changes; when our way of living changes, our relationships and ministry change. Zacchaeus wasn't required to become good before he could welcome Jesus; he welcomed Jesus and then became good. A home where Jesus reigns naturally becomes a lampstand for the gospel, and all the glory goes to him.
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10). The crowd grumbled that he had gone to stay at a sinner's house, but he cared nothing for his reputation, only for the lost. Jesus stopped first, called the name first, and entered the door first. He is our example for opening our home to unbelieving family and friends.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for calling us by name and being willing to stay in our home. We welcome you joyfully; please turn every corner of our home upside down. And use our home as a place where unbelieving family and friends meet you. May salvation come to their homes too. Amen.
teach: Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector and a rich man, yet in the city of Jericho everyone despised him. He climbed a tree hoping to see Jesus, and to his surprise Jesus stopped and called him by name: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house” (Luke 19:5). Jesus himself took the initiative to enter his home. The most beautiful thing about the gospel is that Jesus doesn't wait for people to become good first; he is willing to walk into an imperfect home.

Zacchaeus “hurried, came down, and received him joyfully” (Luke 19:6). Having welcomed Jesus, his life changed at once: “half of my goods I give to the poor. If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much” (Luke 19:8). When Jesus moved in, Zacchaeus' view of money, his relationships, and his attitude toward the poor were all turned upside down. A home that truly welcomes Jesus will always overflow with blessing and light up the people around it.

Jesus declared, “Today, salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:9). This week we have seen that a home is a lampstand, that its door should be open, that husband and wife can work together, and that witness begins with our own people.
