The starting point of all of this is letting Jesus move into our home first. When he reigns in our home, it becomes not only our shelter from the storm, but also a place where others meet him.
q: Since Jesus moved into my home, what part of my life has he not yet turned upside down?
Is there someone around me who, like Zacchaeus, is overlooked or disliked, yet is searching for Jesus?
talk: Of this week's lessons, what most made you want our home to become a lampstand for the gospel?
This month, for which family could we do one specific thing, so that the good news of salvation has a chance to reach their home?
acts: Say together: “Lord Jesus, please stay at our house today.”
Prepare a small gift for a family who doesn't yet believe
Confirm which family you'll invite for this weekend's date card, and when
lessons.noon: “Today, salvation has come to this house” — Lord Jesus, right now may your salvation come to our home.

mem.t: The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.

s: Take a sheet of paper, write both your names in the middle, and next to them write “2”: besides each other, which one or two couples or friends are spiritual companions you can pray with and who spur you on?
At the top write “3”: who has been, or could become, your spiritual parents? At the bottom write “3” as well: who might God be entrusting to you as spiritual children to walk alongside?
Around the outside write “5”: in your church or fellowship, who do you serve and fight alongside? Think about your place on the team.
Looking at the map, thank God for every name on it; where there are blank spaces, ask God together to provide, and then read 2 Timothy 2:2 together.

lessons.title: A Four-Generation Relay
lessons.theme: The gospel reaches the next generation when we entrust what we've received to others

v: You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.
The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.

lessons.still: Think back over your life since you came to faith. Who has placed God's Word, and an example of a godly life, into your hands? Quietly picture their faces, call each of them by name, and give thanks to the Lord.
lessons.light: 321 Light: 235 is how God builds his order: 2, spiritual companions who support each other; 3, spiritual parents and children who pass on life; 5, spiritual comrades-in-arms who fight side by side. The last of the eight steps to “change your mindset and your life will change” is multiplication: a life that has truly been changed will always go on to influence another life.
lessons.jesus: Jesus appointed twelve disciples “that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach” (Mark 3:14). He first lived and walked with them for more than three years, and then handed them the mission. Jesus didn't leave behind only sermons; he left behind a group of people whose lives had been shaped by his.
lessons.pray: Gracious Lord, thank you for placing the gospel and new life in our hands through so many faithful people. Strengthen us in your grace, so that we don't only receive but are also willing to faithfully entrust what we've received to the next generation and the next couple, so that your life is passed on from generation to generation. Amen.
teach: In a relay race, what matters most is not who runs fastest, but the moment the baton is passed. No matter how fast you run, if the baton is dropped, the whole team loses. At the end of his life, Paul wrote to his spiritual son Timothy: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). There are four generations in this one verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful people, and others.

Paul didn't want an audience of admirers; he wanted a lifeline that would keep on going. The gospel has reached us today not because of one great person, but because for two thousand years, generation after generation of ordinary people have handed the baton to the next person. We can read this lesson today because someone once handed the baton to us: perhaps the friend who led us to faith, perhaps the older believer who read the Bible with us.

Before he speaks of passing the baton, Paul says, “be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 2:1). Spiritual legacy doesn't depend on our ability, but on grace. As we near the end of this year as couples, having journeyed from understanding marriage as God designed it to practicing the self-emptied life and praying as one, God now invites us one step further: to entrust what we've received in our marriage to the next couple.
q: In my spiritual life, who has handed the “baton” to me? Have I ever properly thanked them?
Have I been holding on to the baton in my hand without ever thinking of passing it to the next person?
talk: Looking back on this year in our marriage, what do you think is the most precious lesson God has given us? Who should we pass that lesson on to?
If we're one leg of a relay race, do you think we're still “receiving the baton” right now, or are we ready to start “passing it on”?
acts: Send a message thanking someone who led you to faith or helped you grow
Write down the biggest thing you've received in your marriage this year
Pray for someone you might pass the baton to
lessons.noon: “be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus” — Lord, right now I am strengthened by your grace.

lessons.title: 2: Spiritual Companions
lessons.theme: Your spouse is your first companion, and couples need fellow travelers too

v: Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance.
Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works,
not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching.

lessons.still: Look at your spouse beside you, or picture their face in your mind. Quietly thank the Lord: “Lord, thank you for giving me this closest companion. And please don't let us walk this road alone.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Not wanting others to see our family's struggles comes from fear of losing face; it is the self-ruled life protecting itself. Only when we humbly admit we need companions do we receive support. Humility draws out humility: when we open up first, other couples will open up too.
lessons.jesus: Jesus told his disciples, “I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you” (John 15:15). He is Lord, yet he chose to be a friend to people and openly share his heart. Jesus shows us that true companionship is built on openness and trust.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for giving us to each other as closest spiritual companions. Make us like iron sharpening iron, provoking one another to love and good works. Provide couples to walk alongside us, so that we are not alone in hard times and have someone to hold us up when we are weak, as we walk your way together. Amen.
teach: Two knives lying quietly in a drawer will only slowly rust; pick them up and sharpen one against the other, and they grow sharper and sharper. Proverbs says, “Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend's countenance” (Proverbs 27:17). Sharpening throws off sparks and makes some noise, but that is exactly the value of spiritual companions: not just saying nice things, but spurring each other on so that each becomes more like Christ.

The “2” in 235 refers first of all to your spouse. God joined husband and wife together to be each other's closest spiritual companion. Yet a couple also needs other couples to walk alongside. Hebrews says, “Let's consider how to provoke one another to love and good works” (Hebrews 10:24). To “consider” means to pay careful attention to the other person and think about them. Spiritual companions remember the struggle you mentioned last week and ask, “So how did it turn out?”

Hebrews continues: “not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is” (Hebrews 10:25). Many marriages aren't destroyed by one great storm, but slowly lose their warmth in isolation. When a couple hits hard times, having one or two other couples they can speak openly with and pray with is like having someone to share a fire with in the dead of winter. Lonely marriages grow cold easily; marriages that have companions stay warmer.
q: Do I see my spouse as a spiritual companion? Or only as a roommate in life, or a partner in household chores?
When our marriage runs into difficulties, do we have companions we can open up to? If not, what is holding me back?
talk: What would you like more of in the way we accompany each other spiritually? For example, reading the Bible together, checking in on each other, reminding each other.
Is there a couple we could invite to become spiritual companions with us? How could we begin?
acts: Ask your spouse: “How can I pray for you this week?”
Invite a couple to stay ten minutes longer after your next gathering to talk
Write down the names of one or two couples you'd like to walk alongside
lessons.noon: “Iron sharpens iron” — Lord, right now make me a good companion to my spouse.

lessons.title: 3: Spiritual Parents and Children
lessons.theme: Spiritual parents above to support us, spiritual children beside us to walk with

v: For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, I became your father through the Good News.
I beg you therefore, be imitators of me.
Because of this I have sent Timothy to you, who is my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, who will remind you of my ways which are in Christ, even as I teach everywhere in every assembly.

lessons.still: Think of someone who cared for you in your faith like a father or mother. Quietly thank the Lord for providing them. Then ask the Lord: “Lord, is there anyone right now who needs us to care for them like parents?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: “I'm not good enough to lead anyone” sounds humble, but sometimes it is still self-centered, focused on our own qualifications. True humility means returning to our rightful place: admitting I'm not perfect, yet God is willing to use me. The focus is on Jesus, not on myself.
lessons.jesus: On the shore, the risen Jesus called out to the disciples who had fished all night and caught nothing: “Children, have you anything to eat?” (John 21:5). Then he prepared fish and bread for them over a charcoal fire. Like a father, he first took care of their hunger and weariness, and then restored their mission.
lessons.pray: Father, thank you for supporting us through spiritual parents. Provide older believers we can learn from, and make us willing to become spiritual parents to others. We are not perfect, but we are willing to share honestly how we have fallen and been lifted up by you, pointing to you and not to ourselves. Amen.
teach: A child can have many teachers, but only one set of parents. Teachers pass on knowledge; parents give life. Paul told the church in Corinth, “For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don't have many fathers” (1 Corinthians 4:15). The church has no shortage of people who can explain things; what it lacks are people willing to walk alongside others over the long haul like parents, to worry about them, and to pay the cost.

The “3” in 235 points in two directions: upward, we need spiritual parents; downward, we are to become spiritual parents to others. Paul himself experienced both. When he first came to faith, the disciples were all afraid of him, “But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles” (Acts 9:27). Barnabas was Paul's spiritual guide; later Paul called Timothy “my beloved and faithful child in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 4:17). That is how life passes from one generation to the next.

Spiritual parents don't want people to admire them; they point to Christ. Paul said, “I beg you therefore, be imitators of me” (1 Corinthians 4:16), because he himself was imitating Christ. Spiritual parents don't have to be perfect either; they only need to have walked a little further down the road, and to share honestly how they have fallen and been lifted up by the Lord. A couple married ten years can walk alongside a couple married one year.
q: Have I had a spiritual parent on my faith journey? If not, am I willing to ask God for one?
Is there a voice in my heart saying “I'm not qualified yet” that keeps me from becoming someone's spiritual parent?
talk: Who has walked alongside us like spiritual parents? What one thing they did do you remember most?
Which part of the road we've traveled since our wedding could we share with couples younger than us?
acts: Call or message a spiritual elder to say thank you
Write down an experience you could share with a younger couple
Ask God to show you someone who needs someone to walk alongside them
lessons.noon: “you don’t have many fathers” — Lord, right now give me a parent's heart.

lessons.title: 5: Spiritual Comrades-in-Arms
lessons.theme: Couples find their place in the body of Christ and fight side by side with all the saints

v: He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers;
for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ,
until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a full grown man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ,

Only let your way of life be worthy of the Good News of Christ, that whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear of your state, that you stand firm in one spirit, with one soul striving for the faith of the Good News;

lessons.still: Picture an army in which everyone stands at their post, looking out for and watching over one another. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, where is our post as a couple on your team?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The most common breach in ministry is pride: comparing whose gift is greater and who has done more. When pride meets pride, the team splits. Only the self-emptied can be united, and only the united can overcome. When we let Jesus reign and everyone returns to their rightful place, the team has strength.
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane, Jesus told his disciples, “Stay here and watch with me” (Matthew 26:38). Even in his hardest battle, the Son of God invited companions to keep watch beside him. Jesus shows us that spiritual battle is not a solo fight.
lessons.pray: Jesus, our Commander, thank you for placing us in your body and not leaving us to fight alone. Help us as a couple find our post, stand firm in one spirit with all the saints, and strive together for the Good News. Take away the comparing and score-keeping in our hearts, and make us one in you. Amen.
teach: A soccer team can't be all goalkeepers or all strikers. Every position matters, and only by working together can the team win. Paul says that Christ gave “some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers” (Ephesians 4:11). These five gifts are often called the fivefold ministry, and their purpose is not for a few people to do all the work, but “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12).

The “5” in 235 is about spiritual comrades-in-arms: forming a team in the body of Christ with people of different gifts, to accomplish together what God has entrusted to us. Not every couple has to hold one of these offices, but every couple is a member of the team. Some homes are gifted at hospitality, some at caring for others, some at teaching, some at leading people to faith. When a couple finds their post, their marriage is no longer just about the two of them; it becomes part of the Kingdom.

Paul longed for the church to “stand firm in one spirit, with one soul striving for the faith of the Good News” (Philippians 1:27). The Greek word for “striving” here is an athletic term, meaning to compete shoulder to shoulder like teammates. Spiritual comrades-in-arms don't just have coffee together; they watch over one another in prayer, in service, and in spiritual battle. The goal is “until we all attain to the unity of the faith” (Ephesians 4:13).
q: In my church or fellowship, am I more like a spectator or a team member? What keeps me in the stands?
In serving, have I ever lost unity with others because of comparing or keeping score?
talk: With our gifts combined, which post do you think we're best suited for in our church or fellowship?
Who around us are spiritual comrades-in-arms we can pray and serve with? How can we support them more?
acts: Write down one post the two of you could take up in your church
Write a word of encouragement to a fellow servant or pastor
Pray together once for your small group or ministry team
lessons.noon: “with one soul striving for the faith of the Good News” — Lord, right now make me one in heart with my brothers and sisters.

lessons.title: A Grain of Wheat Falls into the Earth
lessons.theme: Life shapes life; love that pays the price bears much fruit

v: Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.
Do the things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me, and the God of peace will be with you.

lessons.still: Gently set down something you are holding, and open your empty hands. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, I am willing to let go of myself, so that you can use my life to bear fruit.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: To “die” is to be self-emptied: not seeking fame, credit, or reward for ourselves. Self-emptied doesn't mean ending up with nothing; it means entering the limitless. A grain of wheat dies, yet gains many grains. Life first, then relationships, then ministry; only a changed life can multiply life.
lessons.jesus: Jesus told his disciples, “I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15:16). Bearing fruit is not our own plan; it is the Lord's choosing and appointing. Because he first fell into the earth for us, we can bear fruit that lasts.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for falling into the earth like a grain of wheat and laying down your life for us, so that we might have life. We are willing to let go of our comfort and our calculations, so that your life can influence another life through us. Let the fruit we bear remain forever, and may all the glory go to you. Amen.
teach: If a grain of wheat is kept in a beautiful box, it will only ever be one grain. Jesus said, “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). This was Jesus foretelling his own cross, and it is also the principle behind all spiritual multiplication: for a life to influence another life, it must give itself.

Paul says, “Do the things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me” (Philippians 4:9). Notice those four verbs; of them, what people “saw” is the hardest to fake. The most powerful kind of spiritual legacy isn't a course; it is a life that can be seen. What a young couple learns from us is often not what we said, but seeing how we kept loving each other in hard times.

This week we've seen the whole picture of 235: our spouse and companion couples are the “2,” spiritual parents and children are the “3,” and the church team is the “5.” This isn't a formula to memorize but a map of relationships. A grain of wheat in the ground may show no visible results for a while, but God promises that “it bears much fruit.” Walking alongside people takes time, tears, and patience, but bearing fruit is God's work.
q: Is there any part of my life that is like a grain of wheat kept in a box, which I'm unwilling to let fall into the ground?
If someone did exactly what they have “seen” in me, what would they learn?
talk: Looking at the 235 map we drew this week, which direction do you think most needs us to take a first step?

What are we willing to give, concretely, to walk alongside a couple? For example, one evening a month. (If your spouse can't join you at the moment, write down one thing you are willing to give yourself.)
acts: Complete this weekend's 235 map together with your spouse
Choose one direction and write down the first person to contact
Pray for someone who might become a spiritual son or daughter
lessons.noon: “But if it dies, it bears much fruit” — Lord, right now I am willing to let go of myself and bear fruit for you.

mem.t: Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.

date.t: Thanking Those Who Walked with Us
s: Look back together: from dating to marriage to today, which older believer or which couple walked alongside us? Each of you share one small thing they did.
Together, write a thank-you message or card to them, saying specifically how that thing helped your marriage.
Then think together of a couple younger than you who might need someone to walk with them, and set a date to invite them for a meal or a cup of tea.
Holding hands, read 1 Thessalonians 2:8 and ask God to give you a heart as gentle as a mother's and as steady as a father's.

lessons.title: Like a Nursing Mother
lessons.theme: Walking alongside others means sharing not just principles, but our lives

v: But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children.
Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.
As you know, we exhorted, comforted, and implored every one of you, as a father does his own children,
to the end that you should walk worthily of God, who calls you into his own Kingdom and glory.

lessons.still: Picture a mother holding her baby late at night, feeding the child, tired yet tender. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, give me a heart like this to love the people you have entrusted to me.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Giving people principles without giving them our lives is living from the head by ourselves; being willing to share our lives is living from the heart by the Spirit. People matter more than tasks: the goal of walking alongside a couple isn't to finish a course, but for them to feel loved and be brought to Jesus.
lessons.jesus: When two men asked Jesus where he was staying, he said, “Come and see” (John 1:39). “They came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day.” Jesus' disciple-making began not from a pulpit, but by inviting people into his life.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking with us to this day with a mother's tenderness and a father's steadiness. Give us hearts like that, so that we give people not only principles but also our lives and our time. Make our home a place where young couples can come and see, come and learn, and come to be loved. Amen.
teach: When a mother feeds her baby, she doesn't set a bottle down beside the infant and walk away; she holds the child close and warms them with her own body. Paul described his time among the Thessalonians this way: “we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children” (1 Thessalonians 2:7). This hard-edged Pharisee, who had once persecuted the church, was so changed by the gospel that he described his ministry in terms of a mother.

Paul goes on: “we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls” (1 Thessalonians 2:8). Walking alongside a young couple isn't just teaching them a few communication skills or money principles; it's letting them into our lives, so they see how we argue, how we make up, how we pray at the dinner table. Principles can be read in books, but life is passed on by spending time together.

Paul also says that he “exhorted, comforted, and implored every one of you, as a father does his own children” (1 Thessalonians 2:11). We need both a mother's tenderness and a father's steadiness. When walking alongside young couples, sometimes we need to listen tenderly to their hurts, and sometimes we need to remind them firmly to come back to God's Word. A husband and wife walking with others together can complement each other perfectly.
q: Am I more used to giving people principles, or am I willing to let people into my life? What makes me reluctant to let people see my home?
Between a mother's tenderness and a father's steadiness, which do I lack more?
talk: When it comes to walking alongside others, which of us do you think is more tender, and which more steady? How can we complement each other?
If a young couple came to our home for a meal, what would you hope they take away from our home?
acts: Write down one family habit you'd be willing to let others “come and see”
Send a warm message to a young couple
Pray for a newlywed couple by name
lessons.noon: “not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls” — Lord, right now make me willing to share my life with others.

lessons.title: The Older Leading the Younger
lessons.theme: Every season we've walked through can become a signpost for someone else

v: and that older women likewise be reverent in behavior, not slanderers nor enslaved to much wine, teachers of that which is good,
that they may train the young wives to love their husbands, to love their children,
to be sober minded, chaste, workers at home, kind, being in subjection to their own husbands, that God’s word may not be blasphemed.
Likewise, exhort the younger men to be sober minded.
In all things show yourself an example of good works. In your teaching, show integrity, seriousness, incorruptibility,

lessons.still: Think back to when you were newly married. What did you understand least, and where did you keep running into walls? What did you most wish someone would tell you back then? Quietly bring those feelings before the Lord.
lessons.light: 321 Light: “We still have plenty of problems ourselves” often becomes our excuse for not walking alongside others. But what God wants us to pass on is not perfection, but grace. Proud people are afraid of showing weakness; humble people are glad to share how they've fallen, because that is the clearest testimony to God's grace.
lessons.jesus: Jesus taught the crowds in parables, “but privately to his own disciples he explained everything” (Mark 4:34). He was willing to spend private time explaining things in detail to a few. Jesus shows us that passing on life often happens in private, long-term, small-group companionship.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you that no stretch of the road we've traveled has been wasted. Make us people who walk ahead and turn back to warn others, teaching what is good and showing an example of good works. Help us to be trustworthy and careful with our words, so that your Word is honored because of our home, and not blasphemed. Amen.
teach: When hiking, the person in front often turns back to warn those behind: “The rocks are slippery here; be careful!” They aren't necessarily the strongest; they've just walked that stretch a little earlier. Paul told Titus to urge the older women to be “teachers of that which is good, that they may train the young wives to love their husbands, to love their children” (Titus 2:3–4), and he told Titus himself, “In all things show yourself an example of good works” (Titus 2:7). The church was always meant to be a family that passes things on from generation to generation.

Notice that Paul didn't leave the teaching of younger people to pastors alone; he entrusted it to everyone who had walked further down the road. “Older” isn't necessarily about age, but about experience: a couple married ten years can walk alongside newlyweds; those who have come through the years of raising young children can walk alongside those in the thick of it; those who have come through a valley can walk alongside those in one now. We don't need to be experts; we only need to share honestly the road we have traveled.

Paul specifically says the older women should be “not slanderers” (Titus 2:3): those who walk alongside others must be trustworthy. As for the phrase “being in subjection to their own husbands” (Titus 2:5), it must be understood within the whole teaching of mutual submission; it has never meant that anyone should endure violence or control. The responsibility of those who walk alongside others is to pass on God's Word in the right way, “that God's word may not be blasphemed” (Titus 2:5).
q: When we were newly married, which experience, had someone told us about it in advance, would have saved us a lot of wasted effort?
Am I someone young couples can trust? Can I keep a confidence?
talk: What are the three most precious lessons we've learned along the way? Which one is best to share with young couples?
Which stage of marriage do you think we're best suited to walk alongside: newlyweds, couples raising young children, or couples going through a valley?
acts: Write down three marriage lessons you'd like to share with young couples
Today, don't pass along any private matters about anyone else's family
Write down the stage of marriage you're best suited to walk alongside
lessons.noon: “In all things show yourself an example of good works” — Lord, right now let my life be a signpost for others.

lessons.title: Weep First, Then Speak
lessons.theme: The posture of walking alongside: listen and empathize first, then support gently

v: Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep.
Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.
Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.

lessons.still: Remember a time when you were going through something hard and someone simply sat quietly beside you. What did you feel then? Quietly ask the Lord to make you that kind of person too.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Rushing to give answers often comes from wanting to look wise, a hidden form of the self-ruled life. Self-emptied companionship keeps the focus on the other person and on Jesus. And we must “look to ourselves”: while walking alongside others, we must also guard our own marriage and heart, never growing proud or overstepping boundaries.
lessons.jesus: At Lazarus' tomb, even though Jesus knew he was about to raise him, it still says, “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). He didn't begin by teaching about resurrection; he first wept with those who were weeping. Jesus shows us that true comfort begins by stepping into someone's grief.
lessons.pray: Compassionate Lord, thank you for weeping with us when we weep. Make us people who listen, who rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep. When we walk alongside those who have stumbled, give us a spirit of gentleness, help us look to ourselves, and help us bear burdens together and so fulfill the law of Christ. Amen.
teach: If a doctor writes a prescription the moment a patient sits down, the patient won't feel cared for, only dismissed. Walking alongside young couples is the same; we are often in a hurry to give answers. Paul says, “Rejoice with those who rejoice. Weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). Weep with them first, rejoice with them first, so they know “you understand me,” and only then will they be able to hear what we say.

When Job's three friends came to see him, “they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him” (Job 2:13). Those seven days were the best thing they did; later, when they opened their mouths and rushed to explain and judge, they actually wounded Job. The ability most needed in walking alongside others is often not speaking but listening: not rushing to analyze who is right and who is wrong, not rushing to take sides, but first letting both people be heard.

When a young couple really has stumbled, Paul says, “you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren't tempted” (Galatians 6:1). The Greek word for “restore” was also used in medicine, for setting a dislocated bone back in place; it takes gentleness, not force. “Bear one another's burdens” (Galatians 6:2): walking alongside means carrying the load together, not standing on the sidelines giving directions.
q: When someone pours their heart out to me, do I usually listen first, or rush to give advice?
Have I ever taken sides too quickly in someone else's marriage problems?
talk: When you're sad, what do you most want me to do? What do you least want me to do? This can help us understand better how to walk alongside others.
Could we agree on a principle for walking alongside others? For example, “listen all the way through, don't take sides, pray together.”
acts: Today, when your spouse is talking, listen all the way through before you respond
Ask a friend, “How have you been lately?” and then listen quietly
Write down three principles for walking alongside others together with your spouse
lessons.noon: “Bear one another’s burdens” — Lord, right now make me willing to carry burdens together with others.

lessons.title: The Friend of the Bridegroom
lessons.theme: Those who walk alongside others need boundaries: never replacing God, never controlling people

v: You yourselves testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ,’ but, ‘I have been sent before him.’
He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore my joy is made full.
He must increase, but I must decrease.
I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.
So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.

lessons.still: Picture the best man standing beside the groom at a wedding: full of joy, yet knowing that today is not about him. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, in the lives of those I walk alongside, be the one at the center.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Wanting to be the savior of someone else's marriage is leaving our rightful place and trying to take God's place. Let people be people, and let God be God: we only plant and water; it is God who makes things grow. The more self-emptied the one walking alongside is, the more clearly the other person can see Jesus reign.
lessons.jesus: After the miracle of the five loaves and two fish, when the crowd was about to make him king by force, Jesus “withdrew again to the mountain by himself” (John 6:15). He was not pulled along by the crowd's expectations, and he often “withdrew himself into the desert and prayed” (Luke 5:16). Jesus had clear boundaries because he listened only to the Father's heart.
lessons.pray: Lord, you are the Bridegroom; we are only the friends of the Bridegroom. As we walk alongside others, let us rejoice in seeing them draw closer to you, not in their depending on us. Give us wisdom to keep boundaries, to protect people's privacy, and to know our own limits. May you increase and we decrease, and may everything go to you, the One who gives the increase. Amen.
teach: John the Baptist's disciples were worried that everyone was going off to follow Jesus, but John said, “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom's voice” (John 3:29). Those who walk alongside young couples are like the friend of the bridegroom: our joy is not in how much they depend on us, but in their growing closer to Christ. That's why John said, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

Paul says, “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6). This brings out the boundaries of walking alongside others: we can share, remind, and pray, but we don't make decisions for them, don't control their lives, and don't let them depend on us more than on God. We must protect their privacy and never spread their affairs around in the name of “prayer requests.” When walking alongside someone of the opposite sex, it's best for husband and wife to do it together.

There is one more boundary, the most important of all: knowing our own limits. If, while walking alongside a couple, you discover physical, verbal, sexual, or financial abuse and control, or serious addiction, depression, or thoughts of self-harm, safety always comes first. In those situations, don't simply urge them to endure, forgive, and reconcile; help them connect with a pastor and with professional counseling. Being willing to refer is not failure; it is true love.
q: When I walk alongside or help people, do I enjoy the feeling of being needed, even to the point of wanting them to depend on me?
Have I ever shared someone's private matters with others under the name of “prayer requests”?
talk: If we begin walking alongside a couple, what boundaries do we need to agree on first? For example, time, privacy, and interactions with the opposite sex.
If we run into problems beyond what we can handle, who could we refer them to?
acts: Write down two boundaries you will keep when walking alongside others
Look up counseling resources at your church or nearby that you could refer people to
Pray for someone you walk alongside: “Lord, help them rely on you more.”
lessons.noon: “He must increase, but I must decrease” — Lord Jesus, right now may you increase in people's hearts.

lessons.title: Walking Together on the Road to Emmaus
lessons.theme: Walking alongside means going together, listening, opening the Scriptures, and sharing a table

v: While they talked and questioned together, Jesus himself came near, and went with them.
But their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
He said to them, “What are you talking about as you walk, and are sad?”
When he had sat down at the table with them, he took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave it to them.
Their eyes were opened and they recognized him; then he vanished out of their sight.
They said to one another, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?”

lessons.still: Imagine you are walking down a path at dusk, your heart full of disappointment and questions. A stranger comes up beside you and gently asks, “What are you talking about?” Quietly, let Jesus walk with you.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Spirit · Insight · Life · Service · Glory: first our spirit is lit up by the Lord and we gain insight into the truth; our life is changed, and only then can we serve others, with everything finally going to God's glory. Walking alongside young couples isn't passing on techniques; it is letting the Lord set us on fire first, and then letting that fire spread from our home to another home.
lessons.jesus: After restoring Peter, Jesus said to him, “Feed my lambs” (John 21:15). He handed the care of his flock to a man who had fallen and been won back by love. Jesus shows us that what qualifies us to walk alongside others is not never having fallen, but loving the Lord deeply.
lessons.pray: Risen Lord Jesus, thank you for walking with us yourself on our road of disappointment and making our hearts burn again. Send us to draw near to the young couples around us, to listen to them, share your Word with them, and break bread with them at the table, so that their eyes are opened and they recognize you. Amen.
teach: On the day of the resurrection, two disciples left Jerusalem in disappointment, heading for Emmaus. “While they talked and questioned together, Jesus himself came near, and went with them” (Luke 24:15). Jesus didn't wait at the crossroads for them to turn back; he came alongside them and matched their pace. The first step in walking alongside young couples is likewise to draw near and enter the real rhythm of their lives.

Jesus first asked, “What are you talking about as you walk, and are sad?” (Luke 24:17). He knew everything, yet he let them first speak out the sorrow in their hearts. Only then did he open the Scriptures. Then, when they sat down at the table, “he took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave it to them” (Luke 24:30), and their eyes were opened. Walking together, asking, listening, opening the Scriptures, sharing a table: this is what walking alongside looks like in full.

Finally they said to each other, “Weren't our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32). Good companionship doesn't make people remember how well we talk; it makes their hearts burn for the Lord again. This week we have learned the heart, the ways, and the boundaries of walking alongside others. Now we can invite a couple to set out on this road together.
q: Is there a couple around me walking a road of disappointment, “sad” as they go?
When was the last time my heart “burned” for the Lord? Do I need the Lord to set me on fire again first?
talk: If we invited a young couple over for a meal, what good question could we ask that would make them want to share what's on their hearts?

Which lesson this week most made you want to walk alongside others? Could we set a date for our first invitation together? (If your spouse can't join you at the moment, write down one person you'd like to walk alongside first.)
acts: Decide on a young couple to invite, and a date
Prepare one good question you could ask at the dinner table
Pray for your own hearts: “Lord, set us on fire again.”
lessons.noon: “Jesus himself came near, and went with them” — Lord Jesus, right now please walk with me.

mem.t: He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on his throne.

s: Each of you take ten quiet minutes to write down three moments from this year when “the LORD helped us until now”: a reconciliation, a hard time you came through, and a change.
Take turns sharing. After each one, the other responds: “Thank the Lord. This is his grace.”
Together, choose a stone or a small object, write the date and “Ebenezer” on it, and put it somewhere visible at home as a memorial of this year.
Holding hands, read Revelation 3:21 together and bless each other: “May you be an overcomer and sit with Christ on his throne.”

lessons.title: The Lord Who Knocks, the Promise of the Throne
lessons.theme: Overcoming begins with opening the door and ends with sitting with Christ on his throne

v: Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him and will dine with him, and he with me.
He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on his throne.

lessons.still: Imagine a soft knock at your front door. It's not a salesman or a delivery driver; it's Jesus. Listen quietly, and then say in your heart, “Lord, please come in.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Thinking we're rich and don't need the Lord is the most hidden form of pride. Overcoming doesn't come from reigning by ourselves, but from first letting Jesus reign; whoever lets Jesus sit on the throne of their home, Jesus will one day let sit with him on his throne. Humility is the key to overcoming.
lessons.jesus: On the eve of his crucifixion, Jesus told his disciples, “In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). He didn't say there would be no trouble; he said he had already overcome. Our overcoming is built on the victory he has already won.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for standing at the door and knocking so patiently. We confess that we have been lukewarm and kept you out of certain corners of our home. Today we open every door; please come in and dine with us. Make us, as a couple, overcomers who will one day sit with you on your throne. Amen.
teach: With an old wooden door, when someone knocks, the person inside only has to slide back the bolt and the guest can come in. Jesus said to the church in Laodicea, “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him and will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20). These words were written to a church that was lukewarm, neither hot nor cold, and thought itself rich. Jesus didn't break the door down; he knocked gently and waited for someone to open it.

Many marriages look a lot like Laodicea: lukewarm, getting by well enough, but leaving Jesus outside the door. The first step to overcoming is not trying harder but opening the door: letting Jesus into our dinner table, our arguments, our finances, and our intimacy. He promises to “dine with him”; in Eastern cultures, eating at the same table signals acceptance and closeness. Jesus doesn't want a home that is merely polite with him; he wants a home that shares its table with him.

Then comes an immense promise: “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on his throne” (Revelation 3:21). Today we sit at the table with the Lord; one day we will sit with him on his throne. This year we have been learning to let Jesus reign; at the finish line, he will let overcomers reign with him. This is the greatest hope of a husband and wife walking this road together.
q: In our marriage, which room (which topic or area of life) am I still keeping Jesus out of?
Is our home right now more “lukewarm,” or are we on fire for the Lord?
talk: If Jesus sat at our table for dinner tonight, which area of our home would you most want him to come into?
Thinking that one day we will sit with Christ on his throne, how does that change the way we see the difficulties in our marriage today?
acts: Pause at your front door and tell the Lord, “You are welcome to come in.”
Before dinner tonight, thank the Lord together for being with you
Write down one area of family life you want to invite Jesus into
lessons.noon: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock” — Lord Jesus, right now I open the door to you.

lessons.title: When We Fall, We Rise Again
lessons.theme: Overcoming isn't never falling; it's getting up again with the Lord after we fall

v: But as for me, I will look to the LORD. I will wait for the God of my salvation. My God will hear me.
Don’t rejoice against me, my enemy. When I fall, I will arise. When I sit in darkness, the LORD will be a light to me.
for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again, but the wicked are overthrown by calamity.

lessons.still: Think back to your biggest failure in your marriage this year. Don't run from it, and don't beat yourself up; just gently lay that moment at the Lord's feet and hear him say, “My child, get up.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: When we refuse to get up after falling, sometimes it's self-pity and sometimes it's fear of losing face; either way, the focus is on ourselves. Pride says, “I don't need help”; humility says, “Lord, lift me up.” Humility is the key to revival and the beginning of turning defeat into victory.
lessons.jesus: Jesus knew Peter would deny him three times, yet he told him beforehand, “I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn't fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers” (Luke 22:32). Before Peter ever fell, Jesus had already prepared a mission for him for “when once you have turned again.”
lessons.pray: God of our salvation, thank you for not giving up on us when we fell. We confess there were many failures this year, but we will not stay sitting in the darkness; we will look to you. Lift us up, and when our spouse falls, help us not to gloat or condemn, but to open our arms and rise again together. Amen.
teach: When babies learn to walk, they fall many, many times. No parent ever says to a toddler who falls, “You're just not cut out for walking.” They only crouch down, open their arms, and say, “Try again!” The prophet Micah said, “Don't rejoice against me, my enemy. When I fall, I will arise. When I sit in darkness, the LORD will be a light to me” (Micah 7:8). Overcomers are not people who have never fallen, but people who get up again after they fall.

Proverbs says, “a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again” (Proverbs 24:16). The righteous person here isn't someone perfect, but someone who comes back to God again and again. This year we may have fallen over and over: in our words, our emotions, our intimacy, our finances. What the enemy most wants is for us to believe, “This is just how your marriage is; it will never change.” But God's Word says that falling is not the end.

The secret to turning defeat into victory is in the verse just before: “But as for me, I will look to the LORD. I will wait for the God of my salvation” (Micah 7:7). The focus is not on where we fell, but on the God who saves us. We must also say this honestly: if there is violence or ongoing harm in a marriage, the first step in rising up is to seek safety and help, not to pretend everything is fine. The overcoming God wants is real healing.
q: Is there a fall from this year that I have never really let myself “get up” from before God?
When my spouse falls, am I more like the enemy rejoicing over them, or like a parent opening my arms and saying, “Try again”?
talk: Looking back on this year, when did we fall but get up together by God's strength? What helped us that time?
If you fall again next time, how would you like me to help you “try again”?
acts: Tell your spouse: “When you fall, I'll be there to help you get up again.”
Write down a time God lifted you up after you fell
Pray for someone who still feels like a failure
lessons.noon: “When I fall, I will arise” — Lord, right now lift me up to look to you.

lessons.title: Through Him Who Loved Us
lessons.theme: We overcome not by our own strength, but by Christ's love and by faith

v: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Could oppression, or anguish, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?
Even as it is written, “For your sake we are killed all day long. We were accounted as sheep for the slaughter.”
No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.
For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith.

lessons.still: Slowly read this sentence: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” Let the question echo in your heart. Quietly answer the Lord: “Lord, nothing can separate us from your love.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Overcoming by our own strength is the striving of the self-ruled life; the harder we try, the more exhausted we get. Overcoming through the Lord is the leaning of the self-emptied life. Only the self-emptied overcome: when we stop putting ourselves at the center, Christ's love becomes our strength, and in all these things we are more than conquerors.
lessons.jesus: In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). His victory didn't come from seizing power, but from surrendering his will to the Father in his most agonizing hour. The cross looked like defeat, yet it was the greatest victory in history.
lessons.pray: Lord who loves us, thank you that your love never leaves us, and that nothing can separate us from you. We confess that we often try to tough things out ourselves and only get more exhausted. Today we plug our marriage back into the source of your love; make us more than conquerors in all these things through you. Amen.
teach: No matter how powerful an electric car's battery is, it has to be plugged in to keep running. Love in marriage is the same: our own love runs out, but Christ's love is a source that never loses power. Paul lists seven hardships in a single breath: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Could oppression, or anguish, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?” (Romans 8:35). Any one of them could crush a family.

Paul's answer: “No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37). Notice: it doesn't say these things won't happen, but that we overcome “in all these things.” Overcoming isn't escaping hardship; it is being held tight by Christ's love in the middle of it. The Greek word behind “more than conquerors” means something like “super-conquerors”: not barely scraping through, but coming to know the Lord's love more deeply in the midst of it all.

John says, “This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith” (1 John 5:4). Every theme of this year's course, being self-emptied, the fruit of the Spirit, communication, forgiveness, submission, will wear us out if we rely only on willpower. The secret of overcoming is faith: believing that Christ's love will never leave us, and that his life can be lived out in us. A couple who lean on him together are an overcoming couple.
q: This year, in what area of my marriage have I most often tried to tough it out by sheer willpower?
Is there a hardship right now that makes me feel as if I've been separated from God's love?
talk: This year, when did you most deeply experience relying “through him” rather than on ourselves?
Of the hardships Paul lists, which has our family been through or are we going through now? How can we lean on the Lord together?
acts: Read Romans 8:37 aloud once
Bring one thing you've been toughing out to the Lord in prayer
Tell your spouse: “Through the Lord, we'll get through this.”
lessons.noon: “in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” — Lord, right now I overcome through your love.

lessons.title: The Blood of the Lamb and the Word of Our Testimony
lessons.theme: We overcome the accuser through the forgiveness of the cross and the testimony we speak

v: I heard a loud voice in heaven, saying, “Now the salvation, the power, and the Kingdom of our God, and the authority of his Christ has come; for the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them before our God day and night.
They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death.

lessons.still: Think about whether accusing voices have been echoing in your mind lately: “You're hopeless,” “Your marriage has failed,” “He (or she) will never change.” Quietly bring these voices to the cross and hear the Lord say, “I have already paid the price for you.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: When husband and wife accuse each other, it is pride against pride, playing right into the enemy's hands; when we stand together under the cross, humility draws out humility, and we both win. Our real enemy has never been our spouse. The focus is on Jesus, not on the other person.
lessons.jesus: When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, he didn't debate the devil; he simply said, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God's mouth’” (Matthew 4:4). He resisted the enemy with God's Word. Jesus shows us that our weapon for overcoming is not our eloquence, but God's Word.
lessons.pray: Jesus, Lamb who was slain, thank you that your precious blood has paid all our debts in full. When accusing voices come, remind us to stand together under the cross and stop accusing each other. Give us courage to tell the great things you have done in our home, so that the enemy's lies are exposed and you receive the glory. Amen.
teach: In a court of law, if someone has already paid a defendant's debt in full, it doesn't matter how much evidence the prosecution brings. Revelation describes Satan as “the accuser of our brothers... who accuses them before our God day and night” (Revelation 12:10). What the enemy does most often in marriage is accuse: accusing us in our own minds, and getting husband and wife to accuse each other. Many of the wars in our homes are really the enemy fanning the flames from behind the scenes.

But the passage declares, “They overcame him because of the Lamb's blood, and because of the word of their testimony” (Revelation 12:11). The first weapon is the blood of the Lamb: Jesus' death has dealt with both our sinful nature and our sinful acts. When accusations come, we don't need to argue how good we are; we only need to point to the cross and say, “This debt has been paid in full.” This is also the ground on which we forgive each other, because our spouse's debt has been paid in full too.

The second weapon is “the word of their testimony.” Testimony isn't talking about how great we are; it's telling what God has done in us. Every time we say, “We once went three days giving each other the silent treatment, but God brought us back together,” the enemy's lies are exposed. This year God has done many things in your home; speaking them out is declaring victory. Silence lets grace be forgotten; testimony keeps grace at work.
q: What accusing words have been echoing in my heart lately? Which Bible verse can I answer them with?
Have I ever turned the enemy's accusations into blame aimed at my spouse?
talk: This year, what has God done in our home that we'd be willing to tell others as our testimony?
When we start blaming each other again, could we agree on a phrase to remind each other that “my spouse is not the enemy”?
acts: Write three sentences of testimony about what God has done in your home this year
Share one testimony with a friend
Tell your spouse: “You are not my enemy. We're on the same team.”
lessons.noon: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony” — Lord Jesus, right now I overcome by your precious blood.

lessons.title: Ebenezer: Helped Until Now
lessons.theme: Counting a year of grace; thanksgiving is the mark of an overcomer

v: Then Samuel took a stone and set it between Mizpah and Shen, and called its name Ebenezer, saying, “The LORD helped us until now.”
Praise the LORD, my soul! All that is within me, praise his holy name!
Praise the LORD, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits,
who forgives all your sins, who heals all your diseases,
who redeems your life from destruction, who crowns you with loving kindness and tender mercies,
who satisfies your desire with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.

lessons.still: Quietly let this year pass slowly through your heart: spring, summer, autumn, and now. Together you have completed almost a whole year of lessons. Tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you for leading us all the way here.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Complaining looks at what we lack, and that is the self-ruled life; thanksgiving looks at what God has given, and that is the self-emptied life. When we turn from a human point of view to God's, from the temporary to the eternal, we discover that every step of this year bears the footprints of Jesus. All the glory goes to him.
lessons.jesus: Jesus cleansed ten men with leprosy, but only one came back and fell at his feet to give thanks. Jesus asked, “Weren't the ten cleansed? But where are the nine?” (Luke 17:17). Jesus values thanksgiving, because those who give thanks receive not only healing but a relationship with the Lord.
lessons.pray: God who helps us, until now you have helped us. We count all your benefits this year: forgiveness, healing, reconciliation, renewal. We don't want to forget your grace, nor forget what our spouse has given. Make us a thankful couple, walking with grateful hearts into the final week, and into the future. Amen.
teach: Hikers who reach the middle of a mountain always stop to look back: “We've come this far already!” That one glance gives them strength to keep climbing. After the Israelites defeated the Philistines, “Samuel took a stone and set it between Mizpah and Shen, and called its name Ebenezer, saying, ‘The LORD helped us until now’” (1 Samuel 7:12). Ebenezer means “stone of help.”

Samuel said “until now,” two words that look both backward and forward: God has helped at every step in the past, so we can entrust the road ahead to him without fear. The psalmist says, “Praise the LORD, my soul, and don't forget all his benefits” (Psalm 103:2). We are so forgetful, especially quick to remember hurts and forget grace. That is why we need a stone, a moment, to count God's grace on purpose.

This week we have seen that overcoming begins with opening the door to the Lord, that when we fall we rise again, that through the Lord's love we are more than conquerors, and that by the blood of the Lamb and our testimony we overcome the accuser. Today, let's set up an Ebenezer stone. Next week is the last week of the year; we will stand beside this stone, write down our testimonies of thanksgiving, renew our covenant with the Lord together, and set out again.
q: What is the greatest help God has given our family this year? Have I said thank you to him for it?
Do I find it easier to remember my spouse's faults and forget all they have given this year?
talk: Over this year's course, what do you think is the biggest change in us? Please name one specific thing.

This year, what did I do that you were especially grateful for? And tell me one thing you're grateful to me for. (If your spouse can't join you at the moment, write down one thing you want to thank them for.)
acts: Each write down three things from this year you thank God for
Tell your spouse one specific way they've given of themselves that you're grateful for
Get ready the Ebenezer stone you'll set up this weekend
lessons.noon: “The LORD helped us until now” — Lord, right now I thank you for helping us all the way.

52.title: The Wedding Supper of the Lamb

mem.t: Let’s rejoice and be exceedingly glad, and let’s give the glory to him. For the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his wife has made herself ready.”

date.t: Renewing Our Covenant and Setting Out Again
s: Set out the Ebenezer stone from last week and look back together through this year's lesson titles. Each of you share “the week that changed me most,” then write one page together of your family's testimony of thanksgiving: who we were a year ago, how God has worked, and who we are now.

Face each other, hold hands, and take turns renewing your covenant: “Before the Lord, I make my covenant with you once again: to let Jesus reign in our home, to love you, honor you, and be one with you all my life, and to build a household that belongs to God together with you, until we see the Lord face to face.”

Together, write down the names of one couple you are willing to walk alongside, set a date to contact them, and ask God to make you their spiritual parents, so that you pass on what you have received this year.
Finally, read Revelation 19:7 together and say in one voice: “Yes, I am coming soon. Amen! Yes, come, Lord Jesus!” Close the year with thanksgiving and hope.

lessons.title: The Wedding of the Lamb Has Come
lessons.theme: Human history ends with a wedding

v: I heard something like the voice of a great multitude, and like the voice of many waters, and like the voice of mighty thunders, saying, “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God, the Almighty, reigns!
Let’s rejoice and be exceedingly glad, and let’s give the glory to him. For the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his wife has made herself ready.”
It was given to her that she would array herself in bright, pure, fine linen, for the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints.
He said to me, “Write, ‘Blessed are those who are invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb.’” He said to me, “These are true words of God.”

lessons.still: Think back to your wedding day, to the moment the music started and the doors opened. Quietly imagine that one day an even greater sound will ring out in heaven: the wedding supper of the Lamb. Tell the Lord: “Lord, we are waiting for that day too.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: From an earthly point of view, marriage is just about two people's happiness; from heaven's point of view, marriage exists so that Jesus receives all the glory. “The Lord our God, the Almighty, reigns!” This year we have been learning to let Jesus reign; the destination is his reigning forever.
lessons.jesus: At the Last Supper Jesus told his disciples, “I will not drink of this fruit of the vine from now on, until that day when I drink it anew with you in my Father's Kingdom” (Matthew 26:29). On the eve of the cross, Jesus' eyes were fixed on that banquet. He shows us that hope can keep us moving forward even in suffering.
lessons.pray: Almighty God, Hallelujah! You reign. Thank you for inviting us to the wedding supper of the Lamb, not because we deserve it, but because of the Lamb's grace. Make our marriage a beautiful rehearsal for that wedding, and in our daily self-giving and commitment, may we give the glory to you. Amen.
teach: In the very first week of this year, we began with the first wedding, in Genesis; today we come to the last wedding in the Bible. John heard “something like the voice of a great multitude, and like the voice of many waters, and like the voice of mighty thunders, saying, ‘Hallelujah! For the Lord our God, the Almighty, reigns!’” (Revelation 19:6). The Bible begins with a marriage in Eden and ends with the wedding supper of the Lamb. Human history is not heading toward destruction; it is heading toward a wedding.

Then heaven announces, “Let's rejoice and be exceedingly glad, and let's give the glory to him. For the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his wife has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7). The Bridegroom is Jesus, the Lamb who was slain for us; the bride is the church he purchased with his blood. Again and again this year we have seen that marriage on earth is a shadow of the marriage in heaven. Every time we as a couple lay ourselves down, forgive, and commit to each other, we are rehearsing that eternal wedding.

The angel told John to write: “Blessed are those who are invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). This is an invitation sent by God himself. We receive it not because our marriage is so perfect, but because of the Lamb's grace. Whether your marriage today is beautiful, ordinary, or struggling, this invitation is open to you. This hope gives today's marriage eternal meaning.
q: When I think about marriage, do I usually see it through the lens of what is earthly and temporary, or what is heavenly and eternal?
How do I feel, knowing that I too have received an invitation to the wedding supper of the Lamb?
talk: Thinking back to our wedding, what scene from that day reminds you of the wedding supper of the Lamb?
If our marriage is a “rehearsal” for that eternal wedding, what would you hope others see in us?
acts: Look through your wedding photos together and thank God for that day
Say aloud once: “Hallelujah! The Lord reigns!”
Write down one thing you can do today to give God the glory
lessons.noon: “Blessed are those who are invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb” — Lord Jesus, right now I thank you for your invitation.

lessons.title: A Bride Made Ready
lessons.theme: The hope of seeing the Lord moves us to purify ourselves today

v: For I am jealous over you with a godly jealousy. For I promised you in marriage to one husband, that I might present you as a pure virgin to Christ.
Beloved, now we are children of God. It is not yet revealed what we will be; but we know that when he is revealed, we will be like him, for we will see him just as he is.
Everyone who has this hope set on him purifies himself, even as he is pure.

lessons.still: Picture a bride carefully smoothing her gown before the wedding, because she is about to meet the one she loves. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, to get ready for the day I see you, what do I need to set in order today?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Someone living the self-ruled life only asks, “Does my marriage make me happy?” Someone living the self-emptied life asks, “Is my marriage making me more like Christ?” From the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly: we are not managing a relationship that will one day end; we are preparing a bride who will see the Lord face to face.
lessons.jesus: Jesus told his disciples, “I am going to prepare a place for you. If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will receive you to myself” (John 14:2–3). The Bridegroom is preparing a place, and the bride is preparing herself. Jesus' promise turns our waiting into hopeful preparation.
lessons.pray: Jesus, our Bridegroom, thank you for preparing a place for us, and for preparing us yourself. We confess there is still bitterness, pride, and coldness in our hearts; purify us, and help us learn to be like you every day of our marriage. We long to see your face; may we be a bride made ready. Amen.
teach: Once engaged, a bride begins to prepare: trying on dresses, learning the ways of her new family, getting ready for the life ahead. Because the wedding day is near, her life has a direction. Paul told the church in Corinth, “For I promised you in marriage to one husband, that I might present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). The church today is a bride already promised in marriage, waiting for the wedding.

Revelation says of the bride, “It was given to her that she would array herself in bright, pure, fine linen,” and explains, “the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints” (Revelation 19:8). Notice “it was given to her”: the robe of righteousness is a gift of grace, not something we weave ourselves; yet every godly response we make on earth adds its shine to that gown. Marriage is exactly where God prepares his bride: learning to be self-emptied, to forgive, and to be gentle at home is how we prepare our wedding garment.

John says, “we know that when he is revealed, we will be like him,” and “Everyone who has this hope set on him purifies himself, even as he is pure” (1 John 3:2–3). Hope isn't an escape from reality; it changes reality. Knowing we will see the Lord, we don't want to carry bitterness, lies, or coldness into that day. The purpose of marriage is not only happiness but holiness, as we are prepared together to meet the Bridegroom.
q: If the Lord came today, what is there in my heart that I wouldn't want to bring before him?
In our marriage, what is God using right now to prepare me and make me more like Christ?
talk: This year, what change in me have you seen that is “more like Christ”? Please name one specific thing.
To get ready to meet the Lord, what in our home would we like to “set in order” or “make clean” together?
acts: Confess to God one thing that needs to be made clean
Tell your spouse one way you've seen them become more like Christ
Finish a reconciliation or apology you've been putting off
lessons.noon: “Everyone who has this hope set on him purifies himself” — Lord, right now purify me and make me ready to see you.

lessons.title: Oil in Our Lamps
lessons.theme: Stay watchful and ready; a relationship with the Lord can't be borrowed or put off

v: But at midnight there was a cry, ‘Behold! The bridegroom is coming! Come out to meet him!’
Then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps.
The foolish said to the wise, ‘Give us some of your oil, for our lamps are going out.’
But the wise answered, saying, ‘What if there isn’t enough for us and you? You go rather to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.’
While they went away to buy, the bridegroom came, and those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut.

lessons.still: If you can, light a candle and watch the flame. Quietly ask the Lord: “Lord, is there still oil in my lamp? Is my relationship with you still burning?”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Live from the heart by the Spirit, not from the head by yourself. The oil represents a living relationship with the Lord, not knowledge and not outward religious activity. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: a lamp must first have oil before it can light up a home, and before it can light up others.
lessons.jesus: Jesus called himself the Bridegroom: “Can the friends of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them?” (Matthew 9:15). When he was with his disciples, life was full of joy. Jesus shows us that watchful waiting is not a heavy duty, but the natural expectation of those who love the Bridegroom.
lessons.pray: Jesus, our Bridegroom, we are waiting for you. Keep oil always in our lamps, not by leaning on each other or on a course, but by each of us coming to you personally every day. Make us watchful not out of fear, but because we love you and long to see you. When you come, may we both be ready. Amen.
teach: There's no more helpless moment than discovering during a power outage that your flashlight batteries are dead. Jesus told the parable of the ten virgins: all of them were waiting for the bridegroom, and all of them fell asleep. “But at midnight there was a cry, ‘Behold! The bridegroom is coming! Come out to meet him!’” (Matthew 25:6). Only then did the difference show: some lamps had oil, and some were going out. Normally they all looked the same; the difference only appeared at the crucial moment.

The foolish virgins asked the wise ones for oil, but the wise answered, “What if there isn't enough for us and you?” (Matthew 25:9). It sounds a little heartless, but it points to a truth: a relationship with God can't be borrowed. A husband and wife can pray together and read the Bible together, but neither can believe in the Lord or love the Lord on the other's behalf. However strong my spouse's spiritual life is, it can't replace my own daily fellowship with the Lord. The oil in our lamps has to be topped up by each of us, every day.

“Those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut” (Matthew 25:10). This is a serious warning, and also a gentle invitation. Being watchful doesn't mean staying up all night, tense and afraid; it means being ready as a way of life. The fifteen minutes each day this year of being still, looking, listening, reflecting, talking, and acting have been how we add oil to our lamps. The course will end, but don't stop the habit of adding oil, because we don't know when the Bridegroom will come.
q: When this year's course ends, will my own habit of daily fellowship with the Lord continue? How do I plan to keep adding oil?
Have I ever leaned on my spouse's spiritual life and neglected my own relationship with God?
talk: After the course ends, which daily or weekly spiritual habit do we want to keep? For example, praying together or reading the Bible together.
How can we remind each other to “add oil” without it turning into nagging or blaming?
acts: Set a daily time for fellowship with the Lord after the course ends
Agree with your spouse on one family spiritual habit you'll keep
Tonight before bed, say together: “Lord, we are waiting for you.”
lessons.noon: “those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast” — Lord, right now I want to add oil to my lamp and be ready to see you.

lessons.title: Marriage Is a Signpost, Not the Destination
lessons.theme: Marriage on earth points to eternity, so we should love each other all the more today

v: I saw the holy city, New Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared like a bride adorned for her husband.
I heard a loud voice out of heaven saying, “Behold, God’s dwelling is with people; and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.
He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any more. The first things have passed away.”
For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like God’s angels in heaven.

lessons.still: Imagine you are driving toward a wonderful destination, and beside the road stands a sign pointing the way there. Quietly tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you for our marriage; it points to you.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Treating marriage as everything is mistaking the signpost for the destination, and then our spouse is forced to carry a fulfillment only God can give. Let people be people, and let God be God: my spouse is not my god; Christ is. When marriage returns to its place as a signpost, we are actually free to love each other more deeply.
lessons.jesus: After Lazarus died, Jesus told Martha, “I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in me will still live, even if he dies” (John 11:25). In the face of tears and death, Jesus didn't offer a set of explanations; he offered himself. He is the guarantee of our eternal hope.
lessons.pray: Eternal God, thank you for giving us marriage as a signpost pointing to you. Forgive us for treating our spouse as the destination, expecting them to meet needs only you can meet. In our limited days, help us treasure each other more and love each other well, as we look forward together to the day you wipe away every tear. Amen.
teach: Driving to the coast, when you see a sign that says “Beach 5 km,” no one stops the car under the sign to have a picnic, because a signpost's value lies in where it points. Jesus said, “For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like God's angels in heaven” (Matthew 22:30). This isn't belittling marriage; it is telling us that marriage on earth is a signpost, pointing to a greater and more complete marriage.

Some people feel uneasy when they hear this: “Then will my spouse and I still have a relationship in eternity?” The Bible doesn't tell us every detail, but we know that before God nothing good is ever lost; it is only brought to completion. John saw the New Jerusalem “prepared like a bride adorned for her husband” (Revelation 21:2), and heard that “God himself will be with them” (Revelation 21:3). The signpost will no longer be needed, because we will have arrived.

On that day, “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain any more” (Revelation 21:4). For those who are suffering in their marriage, who have lost a spouse, or who have never married, this is an immense comfort. For every couple, it is also a reminder: since marriage is a temporary signpost, we should love each other all the more today, and not waste our limited days on cold wars and keeping score.
q: Have I made my marriage or my spouse the final source of my fulfillment, expecting them to give me what only God can give?
Knowing that our days of marriage are limited, what would I most like to stop wasting them on, starting today?
talk: Knowing that marriage is a signpost pointing to eternity, how does that change the way you see our difficulties today?
If we only had one more year together on earth, what would you most want to do with me?
acts: Today, drop one small argument that is wasting your time together
Tell your spouse: “Thank you for walking toward eternity with me.”
Pray for someone who has lost a spouse or is suffering
lessons.noon: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes” — Lord, right now I give you my tears as I wait for that day.

lessons.title: Yes, Come, Lord Jesus
lessons.theme: Looking back on the year, renewing our covenant and setting out again as overcoming couples awaiting the Lord's return

v: The Spirit and the bride say, “Come!” He who hears, let him say, “Come!” He who is thirsty, let him come. He who desires, let him take the water of life freely.
He who testifies these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen! Yes, come, Lord Jesus!
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with all the saints. Amen.

lessons.still: This is the last lesson of the year. Quietly let these fifty-two weeks pass through your heart: God's design for marriage, the self-ruled and the self-emptied life, love and the fruit of the Spirit, communication and forgiveness, the family altar and spiritual parents. Tell the Lord: “Lord, thank you for walking with us through this whole year.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Three foundations, two cores, and one purpose all meet today: Jesus is my example; Scripture is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide. Let Jesus reign; let Jesus receive all the glory. Build a household that belongs to God and welcome the Lord's return. This is the life of an overcomer.
lessons.jesus: The risen Jesus sent his disciples to make disciples of all nations, and promised, “Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). He handed us the mission, and he left us his presence. The course has ended, but the Lord's presence will never end, until he comes again.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for walking with us through this whole year. Before you we renew our covenant: to let you reign in our home, to love each other all our lives, and to build a household that belongs to God as one. Help us pass on what we have received and become spiritual parents who walk alongside others. We want to be an overcoming couple, waiting for you to come. Yes, come, Lord Jesus! Amen.
teach: A graduation ceremony isn't an ending but a beginning; that is exactly why in English we call it a “commencement.” Today we have completed a whole year of lessons, but this is not the finish line; it is a new start. The last chapter of the Bible says, “The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’” (Revelation 22:17). The bride says “Come” to the Bridegroom, expressing her longing for the Lord's return; then it continues, “He who hears, let him say, ‘Come!’ He who is thirsty, let him come” (Revelation 22:17), an invitation sent out to the world.

These two “Comes” sum up this whole year. First, we say “Come” to the Lord: looking back on this year, we write our family's testimony of thanksgiving together, and renew our covenant before the Lord to let Jesus reign in our home and build a household that belongs to God together. Second, we say “Come” to others: we pass on what we have received this year by inviting a couple to walk with us as their spiritual parents, so that they too may come and drink the water of life. Overcoming couples are not only changed themselves; they become a blessing to others.

The Bible's final exchange is: “‘Yes, I am coming soon.’ Amen! Yes, come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20). The Lord promises he is coming soon, and the bride answers: yes, come. This year we have learned to be self-emptied, to be one, and to overcome, all for this day: to sit with Christ on his throne and attend the wedding supper of the Lamb. May we, hand in hand, be overcoming couples, filled with hope as we await the Lord's return.
q: What is the greatest change God has made in my life this year? Am I willing to write it down as a testimony?
Which couple might God be placing on my heart, inviting me to say “Come” to them?
